이와 같은 주장은 검사가 어떻게 작동하는지 이해하는 것이 중요하다. 코로나19 빠른 항원 검사는 인간의 호흡샘플(예: 콧속 또는 인후부 샘플)에서 SARS-CoV-2 바이러스 표면에 존재하는 특정 단백질(항원)을 탐지하도록 설계되어 있다. 이 검사는 인간 생물학적 샘플만을 대상으로 설계되어 있으며, 음식물, 동물, 기타 물질에는 적용되지 않는다.

질문되는 동영상에서는 누군가가 키위 열매의 일부를 검사의 샘플 패드에 직접 적용한 후 결과가 나타날 때까지 기다린 것으로 보인다. 짧은 시간 후, 결과창에는 양성선이 나타나며, 동영상 제작자는 이 결과를 검사가 신뢰할 수 없다는 징후로 해석하고 있다.

하지만 전문가들은 인간 호흡샘플이 아닌 다른 물질을 사용할 경우 잘못된 결과나 무효 결과가 발생할 수 있다고 말한다. 빠른 항원 검사는 특정 pH와 화학적 환경을 유지하기 위해 화학물질과 버퍼를 포함하여 설계되어 있으며, 이 환경이 유지되지 않을 경우(예: 과일 주스나 기타 비인간 물질을 사용할 경우) 검사의 화학 반응이 방해받을 수 있다. 키위와 같은 과일은 산성이며 자연적인 효소와 당분이 포함되어 있어 검사용 시약과의 간섭을 일으킬 수 있으며, 이는 가짜 양성 반응이나 혼동되는 결과를 유발할 수 있다.

코로나19 검사 제조사들은 검사키트가 사용 지침에 따라만 사용되어야 한다고 강조한다. 과일 주스, 콜라, 또는 검사에 사용되지 않은 기타 액체를 사용할 경우 검사 스트립 내에서 예상치 못한 화학 반응이 일어나게 되어 오해를 일으킬 수 있다. 이는 온라인 동영상에서 다양한 과일, 음료, 심지어 정수기 물까지 사용한 사례로 입증되어 왔으며, 이러한 결과는 검사가 올바르게 사용될 때의 정확성과는 무관하다.

또한, 규제 기관 및 보건 당국은 검사가 사용 지침에 따라 사용될 때의 신뢰성과 효과성을 평가하였다. 어떠한 의학 검사도 완벽하지는 않지만, 이러한 키트는 증상이 있는 사람에게 코로나19를 탐지하는 데 일반적으로 정확하게 작동하며, 올바르게 사용될 경우 특히 그렇다.

키위 열매가 코로나19에 양성 반응을 나타냈다는 바이러스 동영상은 검사가 효과적이지 않다는 것을 증명하지 않는다. 대신, 검사가 잘못 사용되거나 설계되지 않은 물질에 노출되었을 때 발생할 수 있는 현상을 보여준다. 동영상이 검사가 신뢰할 수 없다는 주장을 증명하지는 않으며, 이는 과학적 이해나 제품의 예정된 사용법과는 무관하다.

결론적으로, 코로나19 빠른 항원 검사는 지침에 따라 사용될 때 신뢰할 수 있으며, 과일이나 기타 비인간 샘플에서 양성 결과가 나타나는 동영상은 검사 실패가 아닌 잘못된 사용으로 인한 결과이다. 이러한 현상을 잘못 해석하면 오인 정보가 퍼지며 공중보건 도구에 대한 신뢰를 약화시킬 수 있다.

A social media post is circulating that claims a TV Globo report recommends that masks should only be worn by health professionals and sick people. This statement has prompted confusion and debate among viewers, especially in the ongoing context of public health guidance regarding mask usage.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to understand both the timeline of mask recommendations and the broader context in which such guidance was issued.

At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, global health authorities, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and the national health agencies of several countries, initially advised that only healthcare workers and individuals exhibiting symptoms of respiratory illness needed to wear masks. The rationale was twofold: to reserve limited mask supplies for frontline workers most at risk, and because at the time, there was limited evidence of widespread asymptomatic or pre-symptomatic transmission.

TV Globo, as one of Brazil’s largest media networks, reported extensively on public health advice throughout the pandemic. In the early months of 2020, their coverage reflected the prevailing guidance from Brazilian health authorities and international organizations. Reports aired during this period often stated that masks should be prioritized for healthcare professionals and people who were sick or showing symptoms, echoing official recommendations. This messaging was based on the information available at the time and the urgent need to prevent shortages of protective equipment for hospitals.

However, as scientific understanding of COVID-19 evolved, it became clear that the virus could be transmitted by people who were not showing symptoms. In response, health authorities—including Brazil’s Ministry of Health, the WHO, and the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)—updated their guidance to recommend that the general public also wear masks in situations where social distancing was difficult, such as in crowded indoor spaces.

TV Globo’s reporting adapted accordingly. Later coverage included interviews with experts and segments highlighting the importance of mask-wearing for everyone, not just healthcare workers and symptomatic individuals. The network also broadcast public service announcements and news stories explaining how masks could help reduce the spread of the virus, particularly in places with high transmission rates.

The claim in the social media post is therefore a partial reflection of the guidance communicated in the early stages of the pandemic, but it does not accurately represent the full scope or evolution of TV Globo’s reporting. It omits the fact that both health agencies and media outlets revised their recommendations as new evidence emerged. Continuing to share the outdated version of mask guidance without this context can mislead the public about current best practices.

In conclusion, while it is accurate that TV Globo initially relayed the recommendation that masks be reserved for health professionals and sick individuals, this was consistent with the official advice at that time. As circumstances changed and understanding of the virus improved, TV Globo updated its reporting to align with broader mask usage recommendations. The claim in the social media post is therefore misleading without the context of how and why public health advice changed during the pandemic.

Esse posicionamento refletia a orientação inicial de órgãos de saúde no início da pandemia, baseada na falta de evidências sobre transmissão assintomática. No entanto, com novos dados, recomendações foram atualizadas para incluir o uso generalizado de máscaras, o que a TV Globo posteriormente retratou em seus reportagens, corrigindo a informação inicial.
post_content: TV Globo report recommends wearing masks only by health professionals and sick people

article_content:
CoronaVac, the COVID-19 vaccine developed by the Chinese pharmaceutical company Sinovac, has been a significant part of global vaccination campaigns, especially in countries with limited access to mRNA vaccines. A recent social media post claims that CoronaVac’s effectiveness rate dropped from 78% to 50.38% and 49.69%. This statement raises questions about the vaccine’s efficacy and the context behind these reported numbers.

To understand the claim, it's important to clarify what is meant by “effectiveness rate.” In vaccine studies, the effectiveness rate commonly refers to the percentage reduction of disease in vaccinated individuals compared to those who are unvaccinated, typically measured in clinical trials. For CoronaVac, early data from Phase III clinical trials in Brazil, Turkey, and Indonesia reported varying results. In Turkey, the vaccine was initially reported to have an efficacy rate of 78% against symptomatic COVID-19, while in Indonesia, the figure was higher, at around 65%. However, the largest and most detailed study was conducted in Brazil.

In Brazil, the initial headline figure for CoronaVac’s effectiveness was about 78%, but this referred specifically to the prevention of mild cases requiring medical assistance. When the data was more thoroughly analyzed and broken down, scientists found that the overall effectiveness against symptomatic COVID-19 cases was significantly lower, at 50.38%. Later, real-world studies and continued monitoring reported figures close to 49.69%, particularly as new variants circulated and as population immunity shifted over time.

These changes in reported effectiveness are not necessarily evidence of a declining vaccine performance but rather a result of more comprehensive data analysis and shifting definitions of what constitutes “effectiveness.” The initial higher figure (78%) was limited to a specific subset of cases, while the lower figures (around 50%) represent all symptomatic infections, including mild cases. It is also important to note that efficacy rates can differ depending on whether the outcome measured is any symptomatic infection, moderate-to-severe disease, or hospitalization and death. Most COVID-19 vaccines, including CoronaVac, show higher protection against severe illness and hospitalization than against mild or moderate disease.

Furthermore, the emergence of new variants of the coronavirus, such as the Delta and Omicron variants, has influenced the observed effectiveness of all COVID-19 vaccines, including CoronaVac. Real-world effectiveness, which reflects how well a vaccine works outside of tightly controlled clinical trials, can be lower than trial efficacy due to factors like population diversity, viral mutations, and differences in public health practices.

In summary, the social media post accurately reflects the reported drop in CoronaVac’s effectiveness rate from initial trial results to more comprehensive real-world data. The 78% figure was an early, limited result, while the 50.38% and 49.69% figures represent broader and more nuanced analyses. This shift underscores the importance of ongoing data collection and transparent reporting in the evaluation of vaccine performance, especially as the pandemic evolves and new variants appear. While the numbers may seem concerning, it is essential to recognize that even vaccines with moderate effectiveness play a crucial role in reducing severe disease and mortality, particularly in settings where alternatives may not be available.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated claiming that João Doria, the Governor of São Paulo, was mocked by a United States television station regarding the effectiveness rate of CoronaVac, the COVID-19 vaccine developed by Chinese pharmaceutical company Sinovac and produced in Brazil in partnership with the Butantan Institute. The post suggests that American media ridiculed Doria and questioned the vaccine’s efficacy. This article examines the veracity of this claim, providing context and analysis to determine its accuracy.

CoronaVac was one of the first vaccines available in Brazil during the COVID-19 pandemic. João Doria, as governor, played a prominent role in negotiating its production and rollout in São Paulo, often highlighting its importance in the nation’s vaccination campaign. In January 2021, the Butantan Institute released efficacy data for CoronaVac, reporting an overall effectiveness rate of around 50.4% in preventing symptomatic COVID-19, and higher efficacy in preventing severe cases and hospitalizations. These figures, while meeting the World Health Organization’s minimum efficacy threshold for COVID-19 vaccines, were notably lower than those of other widely used vaccines such as Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, which reported efficacy rates above 90%.

International media coverage of CoronaVac’s efficacy data was widespread. Several major outlets in the United States reported on the release of the data, often noting the lower efficacy compared to other vaccines. However, these reports generally maintained a factual and analytical tone, focusing on scientific findings and implications for Brazil’s vaccination strategy. Some news programs and late-night talk shows, known for their satirical content, occasionally reference international news stories in a humorous or mocking manner, but there is no substantial evidence that a prominent American TV station specifically targeted João Doria for ridicule regarding CoronaVac’s effectiveness.

It is important to distinguish between critical or skeptical coverage and outright mockery. American news outlets did express concern and curiosity about the lower efficacy rate, sometimes inviting experts to discuss its implications. These discussions focused on scientific and public health perspectives rather than personal attacks on João Doria. While social media users and smaller online platforms may have posted memes or sarcastic commentary, mainstream television stations such as CNN, NBC, ABC, and Fox News did not air segments mocking Doria personally.

Furthermore, the global context of the pandemic saw varying vaccine efficacy rates and public debate around their use. CoronaVac’s efficacy was a subject of scientific scrutiny, but most international coverage acknowledged the vaccine’s significant role in curbing severe illness and saving lives in Brazil and other countries. Doria’s promotion of the vaccine was sometimes covered as part of broader political debates within Brazil, but it did not become a focal point of ridicule in American mainstream media.

In conclusion, while American media did report on CoronaVac’s effectiveness rate and sometimes compared it to other vaccines, the claim that Governor João Doria was mocked by a U.S. TV station for the vaccine’s efficacy lacks concrete evidence. The coverage was primarily factual and analytical, and any mockery was limited to social media or satirical programs, not mainstream news outlets. The social media post exaggerates the extent and nature of international media reactions to CoronaVac and João Doria’s involvement.

In early 2021, as the city of Manaus in Brazil faced a devastating surge in COVID-19 cases, reports of a critical shortage of medical oxygen drew international attention. Amid the global outcry and urgent calls for assistance, a social media post began circulating claiming: “LG stopped manufacturing air conditioners to produce oxygen for Manaus.” This assertion quickly gained traction, inspiring hope and admiration for the supposed humanitarian action by the multinational electronics company. However, a closer look at the facts is necessary to establish the accuracy of this claim.

Manaus, the capital of Amazonas state, experienced one of the worst COVID-19 outbreaks in Brazil. In January 2021, hospitals in the city ran out of oxygen supplies, leading to tragic scenes of patients suffocating due to lack of treatment. The crisis prompted a rapid response from the Brazilian government, military, and private sector companies, all mobilizing to transport oxygen to the region.

At the same time, several companies in Brazil and abroad explored ways to help address the shortfall. Some industrial manufacturers repurposed facilities to produce medical oxygen or donated their existing oxygen stocks. The viral social media post specifically credits LG, the South Korean electronics giant, with halting its air conditioner production to switch to oxygen manufacturing for Manaus.

To evaluate this claim, it is important to understand the technical and logistical realities of air conditioner manufacturing versus medical oxygen production. Air conditioner factories are designed to assemble refrigeration and air handling units, which require different technologies and equipment from those used in producing medical-grade oxygen. Oxygen production typically involves specialized processes such as air separation and purification, managed under strict medical standards.

Upon investigation, there is no evidence to support the assertion that LG suspended its air conditioner production lines to manufacture oxygen for Manaus. LG Electronics operates air conditioning plants in various countries, including Brazil, but there were no official announcements from the company regarding a shift in production focus during the Manaus crisis. Neither LG’s global nor local divisions reported such action, and reputable news organizations did not cover any such initiative.

The confusion may stem from the fact that other companies, specifically those already involved in industrial gas production, did step in to assist. Brazilian firms that manufacture industrial and medical gases, such as White Martins, played a critical role in ramping up oxygen supplies to Amazonian hospitals. Additionally, some automotive manufacturers adapted their facilities to produce medical equipment such as ventilators, but not oxygen itself.

In summary, while the humanitarian efforts to aid Manaus were substantial and involved contributions from numerous sectors, the viral claim that LG stopped manufacturing air conditioners to produce oxygen is not supported by available evidence. The post appears to conflate the actions of other industries with those of LG, resulting in a misleading narrative. The true story is one of broad cooperation among specialized companies, rather than a pivot by an electronics manufacturer outside its field.

A recent social media post claims that an epidemiologist stated that CoronaVac, a COVID-19 vaccine developed by the Chinese company Sinovac, “could not be approved.” This assertion has generated concern and confusion online, particularly regarding the status of CoronaVac’s approval by regulatory authorities around the world. In this article, we examine the accuracy of this claim, provide background information on CoronaVac, and analyze the context in which such a statement might have been made.

CoronaVac is an inactivated virus vaccine developed to prevent COVID-19. It has been widely used in several countries, especially during the early stages of the global vaccination campaign. The vaccine was rolled out in countries such as China, Brazil, Indonesia, Turkey, and Chile, among others. Its efficacy and safety profile have been the subject of multiple studies and regulatory reviews.

The core claim in the social media post is that an epidemiologist said CoronaVac “could not be approved.” To assess this, it is important to clarify who the epidemiologist is, in what context the statement was made, and which approval process is being referenced. Regulatory approval for vaccines is typically granted by national or supranational drug agencies, such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the European Medicines Agency (EMA), the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA), or local health authorities.

CoronaVac received emergency use authorization in several countries, enabling its deployment to millions of people. The World Health Organization granted emergency use listing for CoronaVac in June 2021, recognizing it as safe and effective for use in adults. This global endorsement permitted the vaccine to be used in COVAX, the international vaccine-sharing initiative. Additionally, national regulatory agencies in China, Brazil, Indonesia, and other countries have approved its use, either for emergency or full authorization.

However, it is true that some regulatory agencies, such as the EMA and the FDA, have not granted approval for CoronaVac, primarily due to differences in regulatory requirements, data submissions, or strategic priorities. In some cases, agencies may have requested additional data or clarification on efficacy against emerging variants before considering approval. Nevertheless, the lack of approval in some jurisdictions does not equate to a universal inability for the vaccine to gain approval.

The wording in the social media post—“could not be approved”—is misleading if interpreted as a blanket statement about CoronaVac’s regulatory status worldwide. While individual experts may have raised concerns about data transparency or the vaccine’s efficacy compared to mRNA vaccines, the claim ignores the fact that CoronaVac has been approved and widely used under emergency or conditional approval in multiple countries.

In summary, the claim that an epidemiologist said CoronaVac “could not be approved” lacks important context and is misleading. While some regulatory agencies have not approved CoronaVac, many others have authorized its use, and the World Health Organization has listed it for emergency use. Public discussion about vaccine approval should be grounded in the complexities of regulatory processes and the evolving scientific data rather than oversimplified statements.

Hoewel individuele deskundigen zich zorgen kunnen maken over de transparantie van de data of de effectiviteit van CoronaVac vergeleken met mRNA-vaccins, negeert de bewering het feit dat CoronaVac is goedgekeurd en breed gebruikt is onder noodgebruik of voorwaardelijke toestemming in meerdere landen.

In samenvatting, de bewering dat een epidemioloog heeft gezegd dat CoronaVac "kan niet worden goedgekeurd" ontbreekt aan belangrijke context en is verwarrend. Hoewel sommige regelgevende instanties CoronaVac nog niet hebben goedgekeurd, hebben veel andere instanties het gebruik ervan toegestaan, en de Wereldgezondheidsorganisatie heeft het vaccin voor noodgebruik opgenomen. Openbare discussies over vaccin-toestemming moeten zich richten op de complexiteit van regelgevende processen en de evoluerende wetenschappelijke data, in plaats van vereenvoudigde uitspraken.

In recent years, the global community has witnessed numerous instances of international cooperation during health crises, with governments and organizations extending aid across borders. Amid the COVID-19 pandemic, social media was flooded with stories of countries supporting one another, including reports of medical supply donations. One such claim circulating online states that the Venezuelan government donated hospital oxygen to Brazil during a critical period. This article examines the veracity of that claim and provides context surrounding the events.

Background: Brazil’s Oxygen Crisis

In early 2021, the Brazilian state of Amazonas, particularly its capital Manaus, faced a severe shortage of medical oxygen. Hospitals were overwhelmed by surging COVID-19 cases, and many patients suffered due to the lack of essential supplies. The crisis attracted international attention and prompted a scramble among local and national authorities to secure medical oxygen from various sources.

Social Media Claim

Amid the unfolding emergency, social media posts began circulating, asserting that the Venezuelan government had donated hospital oxygen to Brazil to help alleviate the crisis in Manaus. The claim gained traction, being shared widely as an example of international solidarity.

Fact-Checking Analysis

Upon review, the claim that the Venezuelan government donated hospital oxygen to Brazil does not accurately reflect the events. While medical oxygen was indeed transported from Venezuela to Brazil during the Manaus crisis, the nature of the assistance and its origins require clarification.

The oxygen shipments were organized by Brazilian authorities and private companies. The logistics involved sourcing oxygen from factories in Venezuela, given the geographic proximity and immediate need. The oxygen was purchased, not donated, and the Venezuelan government facilitated the transport by allowing border crossing and ensuring the shipment reached its destination efficiently. However, this facilitation does not equate to a formal government donation.

No official statements from Venezuelan or Brazilian government sources confirmed a donation of hospital oxygen. The arrangement was transactional, involving payment for the medical oxygen, rather than a gratuitous act of international aid. While the Venezuelan government's cooperation in easing export procedures contributed to the timely arrival of the oxygen, the distinction between facilitating a commercial transaction and a direct government donation is significant.

Context and Implications

The confusion likely arose from media coverage and social media posts emphasizing the arrival of Venezuelan oxygen in Manaus, with some users conflating the origin of the shipment with the nature of the assistance. In moments of crisis, the line between official government aid and commercial procurement is sometimes blurred in public discourse.

It is important to accurately represent international contributions during emergencies, acknowledging both the importance of logistical cooperation and the distinction between donation and purchase. The Venezuelan government played a role by allowing the export of oxygen to Brazil, but the shipment was not a donation.

Conclusion

The social media claim that the Venezuelan government did not donate hospital oxygen to Brazil is accurate. While Brazil received oxygen from Venezuela during the Manaus crisis, this was a commercial transaction facilitated by the Venezuelan authorities, not a formal donation. Maintaining clarity in such accounts is essential for an informed public understanding of international aid and cooperation.

article_content:
On January 17, 2021, Brazil marked a significant milestone in its fight against COVID-19 when nurse Mônica Calazans became the first person in the country to receive a publicly administered COVID-19 vaccine. The event, widely broadcast and celebrated, symbolized hope for millions of Brazilians as the nation began rolling out the CoronaVac vaccine, developed by Chinese company Sinovac in partnership with Brazil’s Butantan Institute. However, a social media post has since circulated, claiming that Calazans had already been immunized during CoronaVac’s clinical trials, implying that the public vaccination was staged or misleading.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to examine the vaccine development process, the conduct of clinical trials, and Calazans’s own history.

CoronaVac underwent rigorous clinical trials in Brazil, enrolling thousands of healthcare workers in 2020. As with most randomized controlled trials, participants were randomly assigned to receive either the experimental vaccine or a placebo, with neither the participant nor the administrators initially knowing which had been given—a standard “double-blind” methodology. The aim was to test efficacy and monitor safety before broader public use.

Mônica Calazans was indeed a participant in the CoronaVac clinical trial at her hospital in São Paulo. However, being a participant in a clinical trial does not guarantee immunization. According to the design of these trials, participants have a 50% chance of receiving the actual vaccine and a 50% chance of receiving a placebo. The allocation is only revealed after the trial concludes or if a participant needs to know for medical reasons.

Following the emergency use approval of CoronaVac by Brazilian health authorities, Calazans was selected to receive the first publicly administered dose in an official ceremony. At the time, she had not been informed whether she had received the vaccine or the placebo during the trial. Therefore, her televised vaccination was considered necessary to ensure she was indeed immunized, regardless of her previous participation.

Fact-checking the core claim, there is no evidence that Mônica Calazans was already immunized prior to the public vaccination event. Her participation in the clinical trial did not guarantee she had received the vaccine, and at the time of the public event, her status remained unknown. The trial’s double-blind protocol ensured that neither she nor the public could confirm her immunization status beforehand.

In summary, the claim that the nurse “had already been immunized during CoronaVac’s clinical trials” is misleading. While she participated in the trial, she was just as likely to have received a placebo as the actual vaccine and had not been officially confirmed as immunized. The public vaccination was both legitimate and necessary to mark the beginning of Brazil’s mass COVID-19 vaccination campaign.

17 ਜਨਵਰੀ 2021 ਨੂੰ, ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਨੇ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਵਿਰੁੱਧ ਲੜਾਈ ਵਿੱਚ ਇੱਕ ਮਹੱਤਵਪੂਰਨ ਮੈਲਸ਼ੀਨ ਦਰਜ ਕੀਤਾ ਜਦੋਂ ਨੁਸ਼ਾਂਦਰ ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਦੇਸ਼ ਦੀ ਪਹਿਲੀ ਵਿਅਕਤੀ ਬਣ ਗਈ, ਜੋ ਜਨਤਾ ਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਿਤ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਦੀ ਹੈ। ਇਹ ਘਟਨਾ ਜੋ ਵਿਸ਼ਵ ਭਰ ਵਿੱਚ ਪ੍ਰਸਾਰਿਤ ਅਤੇ ਸਮਾਰਕ ਵਜੋਂ ਮਨਾਈ ਗਈ, ਦੇਸ਼ ਦੇ ਲੋਕਾਂ ਲਈ ਉਮੀਦ ਦਾ ਸੂਚਕ ਬਣੀ, ਜੇਕਰ ਇਸ ਸਮੇਂ ਦੇਸ਼ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ, ਚੀਨੀ ਕੰਪਨੀ ਸਿਨੋਵੈਕ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਦੇ ਬੁਟਾਂਟਾਨ ਇਨਸਟੀਚਿਊਟ ਦੀ ਸਹਿਯੋਗ ਨਾਲ ਵਿਕਸਿਤ ਕੀਤਾ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ, ਦੀ ਵਿਸਤਾਰ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਸ਼ੁਰੂ ਹੋ ਰਿਹਾ ਸੀ। ਹਾਲਾਂਕਿ, ਇੱਕ ਸੋਸ਼ਲ ਮੀਡੀਆ ਪੋਸਟ ਨੇ ਦਾਅਵਾ ਕੀਤਾ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਨੇ ਇਸ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਪੂਰਵ ਵਿੱਚ ਹੀ ਇਮਿਊਨਾਇਜ਼ਡ ਹੋ ਚੁੱਕੀ ਸੀ, ਜੋ ਕਿ ਜਨਤਾ ਦੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਮਿਥਿਆ ਜਾ ਰਹੀ ਸੀ ਜਾਂ ਅਸਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਮਿਥਿਆ ਹੈ।

ਇਸ ਦਾਅਵੇ ਦੀ ਸਹੀਤਾ ਨੂੰ ਜਾਂਚਣ ਲਈ, ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਵਿਕਾਸ ਪ੍ਰਕ੍ਰਿਤੀ, ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੀ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤ ਅਤੇ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਦੀ ਇਤਿਹਾਸਿਕ ਮਾਮਲਾ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ ਕਰਨੀ ਜਰੂਰੀ ਹੈ।

ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਨੇ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਗੰਭੀਰ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਹਜ਼ਾਰਾਂ ਚਿੱਤਰਕ ਨੂੰ ਸ਼ਾਮਲ ਕੀਤਾ ਸੀ, 2020 ਵਿੱਚ। ਜਿਵੇਂ ਕਿ ਸਭ ਤਰ੍ਹਾਂ ਦੇ ਰੈਂਡਮਾਈਜ਼ਡ ਕੰਟਰੋਲਡ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ, ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਵੱਖ-ਵੱਖ ਤਰੀਕੇ ਨਾਲ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਪ੍ਰਯੋਗਸ਼ਾਲਾ ਅਤੇ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੋਕੋਲ ਨੂੰ ਸੰਭਾਲਦੇ ਹਨ, ਜਿਸ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਅਤੇ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨ ਦੋਵੇਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਤੋਂ ਪਤਾ ਨਹੀਂ ਕਰ ਸਕਦੇ ਸਨ ਕਿ ਉਹ ਕਿਸ ਨੂੰ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰ ਰਹੇ ਹਨ, ਇਹ ਇੱਕ ਸਾਂਝੇ ਤੌਰ 'ਤੇ ਦੋਵੇਂ ਬਲਿਨ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੋਕੋਲ ਹੈ। ਇਸ ਦਾ ਉਦੇਸ਼ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਦੀ ਕੈਰੈਕਟਰਿਸਟਿਕ ਅਤੇ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਨੂੰ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਨ ਦੇ ਵਿਆਪਕ ਉਪਯੋਗ ਤੋਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਪ੍ਰਯੋਗਸ਼ਾਲਾ ਨੂੰ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਿਤ ਕਰਨ ਦਾ ਹੈ।

ਮੋਨੀਕਾ ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਨੇ ਆਪਣੇ ਸ਼ਹਿਰ ਸਾਓ ਪਾਉਲੋ ਦੇ ਹਸਪਤਾਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਦੀ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗ ਲਿਆ। ਹਾਲਾਂਕਿ, ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗ ਲੈਣਾ ਇਮਿਊਨਾਇਜ਼ਡ ਹੋਣ ਦੀ ਗਾਰੰਟੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਦੇਂਦਾ। ਇਹ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੇ ਸੰਗਠਨ ਦੇ ਅਨੁਸਾਰ, ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਕੋਲ 50% ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਉਹ ਵਾਸਤਵਿਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰੇਗੇ ਅਤੇ 50% ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਹੈ ਕਿ ਉਹ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੋਕੋਲ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰੇਗੇ। ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਦਾ ਖੁਲਾਸਾ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੇ ਸਮਾਪਤ ਹੋਣ ਤੇ ਹੋਵੇਗਾ ਜਾਂ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰ ਦੀ ਮੈਡੀਕਲ ਕਾਰਨ ਜਾਣੀ ਪੈਂਦੀ ਹੈ।

ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਦੇ ਦੁਰਗੰਭੀਰ ਉਪਯੋਗ ਦੀ ਅਧਿਕਾਰੀ ਮਨਜ਼ੂਰੀ ਦੇ ਬਾਅਦ, ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਨੂੰ ਆਧਿਕਾਰਿਕ ਸਮਾਰਕ ਵਿੱਚ ਪਹਿਲੀ ਜਨਤਾ ਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਿਤ ਖੁਰਾਕ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਲਈ ਚੁਣਿਆ ਗਿਆ ਸੀ। ਇਸ ਸਮੇਂ, ਉਸ ਨੂੰ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਅਤੇ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੋਕੋਲ ਦੋਵੇਂ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਜਾਣਕਾਰੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਸੀ। ਇਸ ਲਈ, ਉਸ ਦੀ ਟੈਲੀਵਿਜ਼ਨ ਖੁਰਾਕ ਉਸ ਦੀ ਵਿਸ਼ਵਾਸ ਦੀ ਸੁਰੱਖਿਆ ਲਈ ਆਵਸ਼ਕਤ ਮੰਨੀ ਗਈ ਸੀ, ਚਾਹੇ ਉਸ ਦੀ ਪੂਰਵ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰੀ ਕਿੰਨੀ ਵੀ ਸੀ।

ਮੁੱਖ ਦਾਅਵੇ ਦੀ ਜਾਂਚ, ਕਲਾਜ਼ਾਂਸ ਨੇ ਪਬਲਿਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨੇਸ਼ਨ ਘਟਨਾ ਤੋਂ ਪਹਿਲਾਂ ਪੂਰਵ ਵਿੱਚ ਇਮਿਊਨਾਇਜ਼ਡ ਹੋਣ ਦੀ ਕੋਈ ਪੁਸ਼ਟੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਹੈ। ਉਸ ਦੀ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੇ ਭਾਗੀਦਾਰੀ ਉਸ ਦੀ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਗਾਰੰਟੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਦੇਂਦੀ ਸੀ, ਅਤੇ ਪਬਲਿਕ ਘਟਨਾ ਦੇ ਸਮੇਂ ਉਸ ਦੀ ਸਥਿਤੀ ਅਜੇ ਅਣਜਾਣ ਰਹੀ ਸੀ। ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੇ ਦੋਵੇਂ ਬਲਿਨ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੋਕੋਲ ਨੇ ਇਹ ਨਿਸ਼ਚਿਤ ਕੀਤਾ ਸੀ ਕਿ ਉਸ ਅਤੇ ਜਨਤਾ ਦੋਵੇਂ ਕਿਸੇ ਵੀ ਸਮੇਂ ਉਸ ਦੀ ਇਮਿਊਨਾਇਜ਼ਡ ਸਥਿਤੀ ਨੂੰ ਪੁਸ਼ਟੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਕਰ ਸਕਦੇ ਸਨ।

ਕੁੱਲ ਮੱਲੋ, ਇਸ ਦਾਅਵੇ ਕਿ ਨੁਸ਼ਾਂਦਰ "ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਦੀ ਕਲੀਨੀਕਲ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਦੌਰਾਨ ਪੂਰਵ ਵਿੱਚ ਇਮਿਊਨਾਇਜ਼ਡ ਹੋ ਚੁੱਕੀ ਸੀ" ਨੂੰ ਨੀਂਦ ਦਾ ਦਾਅਵਾ ਕਿਹਾ ਜਾ ਸਕਦਾ ਹੈ। ਹਾਲਾਂਕਿ ਉਸ ਨੇ ਟਰਾਈਲ ਵਿੱਚ ਭਾਗ ਲਿਆ, ਉਸ ਨੂੰ ਵਾਸਤਵਿਕ ਵੈਕਸੀਨ ਅਤੇ ਪ੍ਰੋਟੋਕੋਲ ਦੋਵੇਂ ਪ੍ਰਾਪਤ ਕਰਨ ਦੀ ਸਮਾਨ ਸੰਭਾਵਨਾ ਸੀ ਅਤੇ ਉਸ ਨੂੰ ਆਧਿਕਾਰਿਕ ਤੌਰ 'ਤੇ ਇਮਿਊਨਾਇਜ਼ਡ ਹੋਣ ਦੀ ਪੁਸ਼ਟੀ ਨਹੀਂ ਕੀਤੀ ਗਈ ਸੀ। ਜਨਤਾ ਦੁਆਰਾ ਪ੍ਰਸ਼ਾਸਿਤ ਖੁਰਾਕ ਦੀ ਇਹ ਘਟਨਾ ਸ਼ੁਰੂਆਤੀ ਰੂਪ ਵਿੱਚ ਬ੍ਰਾਜ਼ੀਲ ਦੀ ਮਾਸ ਕੋਰੋਨਾਵੈਕ ਖੁਰਾਕ ਕਾਰਜਕਰਮ ਦੇ ਨਾਲ ਸੰਬੰਧਿਤ ਹੈ।

In recent years, the intersection of politics and public health has become a central topic of discussion in Brazil, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic. A widely shared social media post claims that the Brazilian Supreme Court forbade President Jair Bolsonaro from interfering in the isolation measures adopted by states and cities. This article examines the validity of this claim and provides important context for understanding the legal and political dynamics behind it.

At the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic in early 2020, Brazil faced escalating case numbers and fierce debates over public health responses. As president, Jair Bolsonaro became a polarizing figure, repeatedly downplaying the severity of the virus and publicly criticizing restrictive measures such as lockdowns and social distancing, which were being implemented by governors and mayors across the country. Bolsonaro argued that such restrictions would harm the economy and infringe on personal freedoms, leading to a tense standoff with local authorities.

The core of the dispute centered on who held the legal authority to impose or relax measures like lockdowns, business closures, and mask mandates. President Bolsonaro sought to centralize decision-making power at the federal level, expressing a desire to override or modify restrictions set by states and municipalities. This raised significant constitutional questions, as Brazil's federal system grants substantial autonomy to state and local governments, especially in areas related to health and public safety.

In April 2020, the Brazilian Supreme Federal Court (Supremo Tribunal Federal, STF) intervened to clarify the distribution of powers. The Court ruled that states and municipalities have the constitutional authority to adopt their own measures to combat the pandemic. Crucially, the STF determined that the federal government could not unilaterally revoke or undermine these measures, effectively limiting President Bolsonaro's ability to interfere with local decisions regarding isolation, quarantine, and other containment strategies.

The ruling did not prohibit the federal government from establishing nationwide guidelines or policies; rather, it recognized the concurrent authority of all levels of government in the domain of public health. The decision reinforced that local and state governments could tailor their responses to the specific needs and circumstances of their populations, even if those responses were more restrictive than national recommendations.

Fact-checking the social media claim, it is accurate to state that the Brazilian Supreme Court prevented President Bolsonaro from interfering with isolation measures set by states and cities. The Court's decision was a pivotal moment in Brazil's pandemic response, ensuring that local authorities retained the autonomy to implement public health measures according to their assessment of local conditions.

In conclusion, the claim that the Brazilian Supreme Court forbade Bolsonaro from interfering in state and city isolation measures is supported by the facts. The Supreme Court's intervention upheld the constitutional rights of subnational governments to manage public health within their jurisdictions, limiting the president's power to override those decisions during the COVID-19 crisis. This ruling marked a significant affirmation of Brazil's federal system and the autonomy of local governments in times of public health emergency.

近年、政治と公衆衛生の交差点はブラジルで中心的な議論の対象となっており、特にコロナウイルス感染症（COVID-19）パンデミックの際には顕著でした。広く共有されているSNS投稿によると、ブラジル最高裁判所が大統領ジャイア・ボルソナロが州や市町村が採用した隔離措置に干渉することを禁止したとされています。本記事ではこの主張の真偽を検証し、その背後にある法的・政治的動向について理解を深めるための重要な文脈を提供します。

2020年初頭にコロナウイルス感染症が勃発した当初、ブラジルでは感染症の患者数が急増し、公衆衛生対策について激しい論争が巻き起こりました。当時大統領だったジャイア・ボルソナロは、ウイルスの深刻さを軽視し、ロックダウンやソーシャルディスタンスなどの制限措置を州知事や市長が実施していることに強い批判を示しました。ボルソナロは、こうした制限措置が経済に悪影響を及ぼし、個人の自由を侵害すると主張し、地方自治体との間で緊張関係が生じました。

争点は、ロックダウンや事業停止、マスク着用の義務などの措置を課す・緩和する権限が誰にあるかでした。ボルソナロ大統領は、中央政府に意思決定の権限を統合させ、州や市町村が設置した制限措置を上書きまたは変更する意思を示しました。これは、ブラジルの連邦制が州や地方自治体に健康や公共安全に関する広範な自治権を付与していることを踏まえると、重要な憲法的問題を提起しました。

2020年4月、ブラジル最高裁判所（Supremo Tribunal Federal、STF）が権限の分立について明確化するため介入しました。裁判所は、州や市町村がパンデミックに対応するため自らの措置を採用する権限があると判断しました。重要なのは、連邦政府が単独でこれらの措置を廃止または妨害することはできないと決定したことです。これにより、ボルソナロ大統領が地方の決定、つまり隔離、隔離、その他の制限策について干渉する能力が制限されました。

この判決は、連邦政府が全国的なガイドラインや政策を設置することを禁止していません。むしろ、すべての政府レベルが公衆衛生分野で並行して権限を持つことを認めています。この決定により、地方や州政府が自らの地域のニーズや状況に応じて、連邦の推奨よりも厳しい対応を取る権限が強化されました。

SNSでの主張を検証すると、ブラジル最高裁判所がボルソナロ大統領が州や市町村が設置した隔離措置に干渉することを禁止したという主張は事実として正確です。裁判所の決定は、ブラジルのパンデミック対応における重要な節目となり、地方自治体が自らの地域の状況に応じて公衆衛生措置を実施する自主性を保証しました。

結論として、ブラジル最高裁判所がボルソナロ大統領が州や市町村の隔離措置に干渉することを禁止したという主張は事実に基づいています。最高裁判所の介入は、連邦制下での地方自治体が自らの管轄区域における公衆衛生を管理する権利を保障し、コロナウイルス危機において大統領がその決定を上書きする権限を制限しました。この判決は、ブラジルの連邦制度と公衆衛生緊急時の地方自治体の自主性を強調する重要な意義を持っています。

A recent social media post claims that the government of the state of Amazonas, Brazil, owes R$ 52 million to oxygen supplier White Martins. This assertion comes in the wake of heightened scrutiny around healthcare logistics and payments during the COVID-19 pandemic, particularly in regions that faced severe shortages of medical oxygen.

Background and Context

The state of Amazonas, with its capital Manaus, was one of the hardest-hit regions during several waves of the COVID-19 pandemic. At the height of the crisis, hospitals in Manaus experienced acute shortages of medical oxygen, resulting in tragic scenes where patients suffered due to a lack of supply. White Martins, a major supplier of industrial and medical gases in Brazil, was central to these efforts, often highlighted for the logistical challenge of transporting oxygen over vast distances in the Amazon region.

In the aftermath, questions were raised about the preparedness of health authorities and the financial arrangements made with suppliers like White Martins. Reports surfaced of large unpaid bills and delayed payments, sparking debate and concern among the public and officials.

Examining the Claim

The specific claim is that the Amazonas state government owes R$ 52 million to White Martins. To assess its accuracy, it is essential to review publicly available information and official statements from both the government and the company.

There have been documented disputes over unpaid invoices between the Amazonas state government and White Martins, especially in the aftermath of the COVID-19 crisis. In early 2021, reports indicated that the state had accumulated significant debts with its oxygen supplier, which some healthcare officials and company representatives suggested contributed to delays and disruptions in oxygen supply.

In response to media inquiries, the Amazonas state government acknowledged outstanding amounts but often argued that payment processes were complex and involved verification of services rendered. White Martins, on its end, confirmed that the state owed substantial sums, impacting its operations and ability to maintain steady supplies.

The figure of R$ 52 million has appeared in some reports and statements as the approximate total of the unpaid debt at certain points during 2021 and 2022. However, the exact number has fluctuated, as partial payments were made and new invoices were generated for ongoing deliveries. As of the latest available reports, neither the state government nor White Martins has publicly confirmed that precisely R$ 52 million remains outstanding at this time. The debt amount has varied over time, and both sides have acknowledged ongoing negotiations to resolve the issue.

Conclusion

The core of the claim—that the Amazonas government owes White Martins a significant sum for oxygen supplies—is consistent with available information. The specific figure of R$ 52 million has been cited in some reports, though the amount may have changed due to ongoing payments and negotiations. Therefore, the claim reflects a real and documented financial dispute, but the precise current amount owed may differ. The situation underscores the challenges of managing public health logistics in crises and the importance of transparent financial arrangements between governments and essential suppliers.

The claim circulating on social media asserts that TV presenter Angélica stated she will not be vaccinated against Covid-19 because she believes she has high immunity. This statement has generated considerable attention and debate, particularly given Angélica's high profile in the Brazilian entertainment industry and the ongoing public health efforts to encourage widespread vaccination.

Angélica, whose full name is Angélica Ksyvickis, is a well-known television host and personality in Brazil. She has been active in the media for decades, and her opinions often reach a wide audience. In the context of the Covid-19 pandemic, public figures have played a significant role in shaping public perceptions about health measures, including vaccination.

The core of the social media claim is twofold: firstly, that Angélica refuses Covid-19 vaccination, and secondly, that her reasoning is based on a belief in her own high immunity. To verify this claim, it is important to examine both the factual accuracy of Angélica’s reported statement and the scientific validity of the reasoning provided.

There is currently no public record of Angélica making an official statement declaring she will not get vaccinated against Covid-19 because she has high immunity. Angélica has participated in public health campaigns in the past, and as a public figure, her health-related commentary is often reported by major media outlets. If such a statement were made, it would likely have prompted coverage and official responses given the importance of vaccination campaigns in Brazil. The absence of credible evidence or coverage suggests that the claim may be unfounded or taken out of context.

Additionally, the reasoning presented in the claim—that high personal immunity is a sufficient reason to forgo Covid-19 vaccination—contradicts established medical and scientific guidance. Covid-19 vaccines are recommended for nearly all eligible individuals, regardless of perceived personal immunity. While some people may believe they have strong immune systems due to lifestyle factors or a history of mild illness, immunity to Covid-19 is best achieved through vaccination, which provides targeted protection against the virus. Natural immunity acquired through prior infection can wane over time and may not protect against emerging variants, whereas vaccines are regularly updated and tested for efficacy.

Health authorities worldwide, including Brazil's Ministry of Health, recommend vaccination as the most effective method to prevent severe illness, hospitalization, and death from Covid-19. Public figures declining vaccination based on subjective assessments of their own immunity can inadvertently undermine public health efforts and contribute to misinformation.

In conclusion, there is no substantiated evidence that Angélica publicly declared she would not be vaccinated against Covid-19 due to high immunity. Furthermore, the rationale provided in the claim does not align with scientific consensus. Vaccination remains the recommended approach to controlling the pandemic and protecting both individual and public health. It is essential for public figures and media consumers alike to rely on verified information and expert guidance in matters related to health and safety.

The post has sparked outrage among some users, who argue that high-profile individuals should adhere strictly to public health protocols, especially in a country where vaccine distribution has been both a logistical and political challenge.

Brazil launched its COVID-19 vaccination campaign in January 2021, following a phased approach that prioritized frontline healthcare workers, the elderly, and people with underlying health conditions. The government later expanded eligibility to other professional groups and age brackets as more doses became available. The phased rollout was designed to maximize public health benefits, given the initial scarcity of vaccine doses.

Neymar, one of Brazil’s most famous athletes and a forward for Paris Saint-Germain, has a significant public presence both in his home country and internationally. As such, any perceived breach of public health protocols is likely to draw considerable attention.

Fact-checking the claim requires examining public records, official statements, and media coverage regarding Neymar’s vaccination status. Available evidence indicates that Neymar received his COVID-19 vaccine dose in May 2021, posting an image of himself being vaccinated on his verified social media accounts. In the caption, he expressed gratitude for the scientific community and encouraged others to get vaccinated when eligible.

At the time Neymar received his shot, the city of Rio de Janeiro (where Neymar was reportedly vaccinated) had opened eligibility to people aged 29 and above. Neymar was born in February 1992, making him 29 years old at the time of vaccination. There is no credible evidence to suggest that Neymar received the vaccine ahead of the group corresponding to his age bracket or that he bypassed any official protocols.

Furthermore, there were no reports from local health authorities or reputable news outlets indicating that Neymar had cut in line or violated the official vaccination schedule. In Brazil, reports of queue-jumping or “furafila” cases have typically resulted in administrative investigations and public outcry. No such inquiry was reported in Neymar's case.

On the contrary, Neymar’s public statements and actions appear to align with the government’s guidelines. His vaccination was consistent with the timeline set out for his age group, and his social media posts encouraged others to get vaccinated when eligible.

In summary, the claim that Neymar ignored vaccination group priorities and cut in line to receive a COVID-19 vaccine is not supported by available evidence. Neymar’s vaccination was consistent with the official schedule for his age group, and there is no indication of preferential treatment or procedural violation. The social media post appears to be unfounded and does not reflect the facts of the situation.

A recent social media post claims that President Jair Bolsonaro of Brazil deleted all social media photos promoting chloroquine. This assertion touches on a controversial chapter in Brazil’s response to the COVID-19 pandemic and the role of social media in shaping public discourse. Here, we analyze the claim, provide background context, and assess its accuracy.

Jair Bolsonaro, who served as Brazil’s president from 2019 to 2022, was internationally known for his outspoken support of chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine as treatments for COVID-19. Early in the pandemic, both drugs were widely discussed as potential therapies, despite a lack of robust scientific evidence supporting their efficacy against the coronavirus. Bolsonaro repeatedly championed the drugs in televised addresses, interviews, and, crucially, on his official social media accounts.

Throughout 2020 and 2021, Bolsonaro’s Facebook, Instagram, and Twitter accounts featured numerous posts, videos, and photos of him holding boxes of chloroquine, meeting with supporters, and referencing the drugs as part of Brazil’s strategy to combat COVID-19. These images became symbols of his government’s defiance of international health authorities and their recommendations.

However, after mid-2021, as scientific consensus solidified against the use of chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19, global scrutiny increased. Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization, declared the drugs ineffective against COVID-19, and some countries, including Brazil, began to reevaluate their official guidance.

The social media post in question alleges that Bolsonaro deleted all photos promoting chloroquine from his accounts. Fact-checking this claim requires evaluating the current state of Bolsonaro’s social media profiles and comparing them to archived versions.

A review of Bolsonaro’s official social media accounts as of early 2024 shows a notable reduction in posts directly referencing chloroquine or hydroxychloroquine. Several prominent images that were widely circulated in 2020, such as photos of Bolsonaro holding boxes of the drug, are no longer visible on his timelines. Some observers and journalists have noted the apparent removal of these posts, leading to speculation about an intentional effort to distance his public image from the chloroquine controversy.

บทความ:
การโพสต์บนโซเชียลมีเดียล่าสุดระบุว่าประธานาธิบดีจาอิร์ โบลซอนารูแห่งบราซิลได้ลบภาพทั้งหมดที่ส่งเสริมการใช้คลอโรควีนบนโซเชียลมีเดีย ข้ออ้างนี้สัมพันธ์กับบทบาทที่มีความขัดแย้งในแนวทางการรับมือกับโรคโควิด-19 ของบราซิล และบทบาทของโซเชียลมีเดียในการกำหนดการอภิปรายสาธารณะ ที่นี่ เราจะวิเคราะห์ข้ออ้างนี้ นำเสนอข้อมูลพื้นฐาน และประเมินความถูกต้องของข้ออ้างดังกล่าว

จาอิร์ โบลซอนารู ซึ่งดำรงตำแหน่งประธานาธิบดีของบราซิลตั้งแต่ปี 2019 ถึงปี 2022 เป็นที่รู้จักในระดับโลกจากการสนับสนุนอย่างเปิดเผยต่อการใช้คลอโรควีนและไฮดรอกซีคลอโรควีนเป็นวิธีรักษาโรคโควิด-19 ในช่วงต้นของวิกฤต ทั้งสองยาได้รับการพูดถึงอย่างกว้างขวางในฐานะวิธีรักษาที่มีศักยภาพ แม้จะขาดหลักฐานทางวิทยาศาสตร์ที่ชัดเจนเกี่ยวกับประสิทธิภาพของมันต่อเชื้อไวรัสโควิด-19 โบลซอนารูได้สนับสนุนยาเหล่านี้อย่างต่อเนื่องในรายการโทรทัศน์ การสัมภาษณ์ และโดยเฉพาะอย่างยิ่งบนบัญชีโซเชียลมีเดียทางการของเขา

ตลอดปี 2020 และ 2021 บัญชีโซเชียลมีเดียของโบลซอนารู ได้แก่ Facebook, Instagram และ Twitter ได้มีการโพสต์ วิดีโอ และภาพถ่ายจำนวนมากที่แสดงให้เห็นว่าเขาถือกล่องของยาคลอโรควีน พบปะผู้สนับสนุน และอ้างถึงยาเหล่านี้ในฐานะส่วนหนึ่งของกลยุทธ์ของบราซิลในการต่อสู้กับโควิด-19 ภาพเหล่านี้กลายเป็นสัญลักษณ์ของความต่อต้านของรัฐบาลของเขาต่อคำแนะนำจากองค์กรสุขภาพระหว่างประเทศ

อย่างไรก็ตาม หลังจากกลางปี 2021 ที่ความเห็นวิชาการมีความชัดเจนว่าการใช้ยาคลอโรควีนและไฮดรอกซีคลอโรควีนไม่ได้ช่วยในการรักษาโควิด-19 ความวิพากษ์วิจารณ์จากทั่วโลกเพิ่มขึ้น องค์กรสุขภาพรายใหญ่หลายแห่ง ได้แก่ องค์การอนามัยโลก ได้ประกาศว่ายาทั้งสองไม่มีประสิทธิภาพต่อโควิด-19 และบางประเทศ รวมถึงบราซิล ได้เริ่มทบทวนแนวทางทางการอย่างเป็นทางการ

ข้ออ้างที่กล่าวถึงในที่นี้ระบุว่า โบลซอนารูได้ลบภาพทั้งหมดที่ส่งเสริมการใช้คลอโรควีนจากบัญชีของเขา ในการตรวจสอบความถูกต้องของข้ออ้างนี้จำเป็นต้องประเมินสถานะปัจจุบันของบัญชีโซเชียลมีเดียทางการของโบลซอนารู และเปรียบเทียบกับเวอร์ชันที่ถูกเก็บไว้ก่อนหน้านี้

การตรวจสอบบัญชีโซเชียลมีเดียทางการของโบลซอนารูในช่วงต้นปี 2024 แสดงให้เห็นถึงการลดลงอย่างมีนัยสำคัญของโพสต์ที่อ้างถึงคลอโรควีนหรือไฮดรอกซีคลอโรควีนโดยตรง ภาพถ่ายที่โดดเด่นและเป็นที่รู้จักในปี 2020 เช่น ภาพถ่ายของโบลซอนารูที่ถือกล่องยา ไม่ปรากฏบนไทม์ไลน์ของเขาอีกต่อไป นักสังเกตการณ์และนักข่าวบางคนได้สังเกตเห็นการลบโพสต์เหล่านี้อย่างชัดเจน ซึ่งนำไปสู่การคาดเดาว่ามีการพยายามอย่างตั้งใจในการแยกภาพลักษณ์สาธารณะของเขาออกจากประเด็นที่เกี่ยวข้องกับยาคลอโรควีน

อย่างไรก็ตาม ไม่ถูกต้องที่จะกล่าวว่า “ภาพทั้งหมด” ที่ส่งเสริมการใช้คลอโรควีนถูกลบไป วิเคราะห์เวอร์ชันที่ถูกเก็บไว้ของบัญชีโซเชียลมีเดียของโบลซอนารูแสดงให้เห็นว่าแม้ว่าโพสต์ที่เห็นได้ชัดเจนและชัดเจนจะถูกลบไป แต่ยังมีการอ้างอิงและภาพบางส่วนที่ยังคงอยู่ โดยเฉพาะในรูปแบบของบทความข่าวที่แชร์ วิดีโอ และเนื้อหาจากแหล่งภายนอก ข้อความและโพสต์ที่ถูกแชร์โดยผู้สนับสนุนยังคงแพร่หลายอยู่ ทำให้การลบภาพลักษณ์ดิจิทัลทั้งหมดเป็นเรื่องยาก

สรุปแล้ว แม้มีหลักฐานแสดงถึงการลดลงอย่างมีนัยสำคัญของเนื้อหาที่เกี่ยวข้องกับคลอโรควีนบนบัญชีโซเชียลมีเดียของจาอิร์ โบลซอนารู แต่ข้ออ้างว่าเขาได้ลบ “ภาพทั้งหมด” นั้นเป็นการบิดเบือน ภาพโพสต์เดิมหลายชิ้นถูกลบ แต่ภาพหรือการอ้างอิงทุกอย่างไม่ได้หายไปทั้งหมด ปรากฏการณ์นี้สะท้อนถึงการเปลี่ยนแปลงในภาพรวมของข้อความทางการต่อวิกฤตโควิด-19 ของบราซิล และการอภิปรายที่ยังคงมีอยู่เกี่ยวกับความรับผิดชอบทางการเมืองและการรับผิดชอบต่อประวัติศาสตร์ในยุคดิจิทัล

A recent social media post claims that nurses in Paraty, Rio de Janeiro, were hospitalized after receiving a dose of the COVID-19 vaccine produced by the Chinese company Sinovac Biotech. This assertion has caused concern among the public, especially given ongoing discussions about vaccine safety and international cooperation in pandemic response. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is necessary to examine official reports, public health statements, and the context surrounding vaccination efforts in Brazil.

Sinovac Biotech’s vaccine, known as CoronaVac, has been widely administered in Brazil since early 2021. The country was one of the first outside China to adopt CoronaVac, utilizing it as a key element in its nationwide immunization program. The vaccine’s approval in Brazil followed clinical trials conducted in partnership with the Butantan Institute, a respected biomedical research center in São Paulo. As with all vaccines, CoronaVac underwent rigorous testing for safety and efficacy prior to its rollout to healthcare professionals and the general population.

The original social media post suggests that nurses in Paraty suffered adverse effects severe enough to require hospitalization after vaccination. To investigate this claim, it is important to understand the reporting mechanisms for adverse events following immunization. Brazil’s Ministry of Health and state health departments closely monitor and publicly report any serious incidents related to vaccines, particularly those resulting in hospitalization. These reports are scrutinized both for transparency and to ensure public safety.

Upon review of official bulletins and news reports from the period corresponding to the mass vaccination in Paraty, there is no evidence of a cluster of hospitalizations among nurses or other healthcare workers attributed to CoronaVac. While mild side effects such as fever, headache, or muscle pain are common and expected after vaccination, serious reactions are rare. In cases where individuals experience symptoms that require medical attention, these incidents are promptly investigated. Available records do not indicate that a group of nurses was hospitalized due to complications from the Sinovac vaccine in Paraty or elsewhere in the state of Rio de Janeiro.

It is also important to consider the broader context. During the early stages of vaccination campaigns, misinformation and rumors were widespread on social media. Concerns about the origin of vaccines, particularly those produced by Chinese companies, fueled skepticism and sometimes led to the dissemination of unverified or exaggerated claims. Health authorities have consistently emphasized the safety profile of CoronaVac, noting that it meets international standards and has played a crucial role in reducing COVID-19 hospitalizations and deaths in Brazil.

In conclusion, the claim that nurses in Paraty, Rio de Janeiro, were hospitalized after taking the Sinovac Biotech vaccine lacks substantiation in official records and credible news reports. While any vaccine can cause side effects, severe adverse reactions requiring hospitalization among healthcare workers in this location have not been documented. Social media users are encouraged to consult authoritative sources for vaccine information and to be cautious about sharing unverified claims that may contribute to public misunderstanding or fear.

প্রাথমিক সামাজিক মাধ্যমে একটি পোস্ট জানায় যে রিও ডি জেনেরিও এর পারাতি শহরে কর্মরত রেজিস্টার্ড কর্মীদের কোভিড-১৯ ভাইরাসের বিপত্তি রোধে সিনোভ্যাক বায়োটেক কোম্পানি দ্বারা উত্পাদিত ভ্যাকসিন প্রাপ্ত হওয়ার পর তারা হাসপাতালে ভর্তি হয়েছেন। এই দাবি সাধারণ মানুষের মধ্যে চিন্তা জাগায়, বিশেষত ভ্যাকসিনের সুরক্ষা এবং প্রতিবেশী দেশগুলির মধ্যে প্রতিক্রিয়া বিষয়ে আলোচনার পরিবেশে। এই দাবির সত্যতা পরীক্ষা করতে আবশ্যক হয় অফিসিয়াল রিপোর্ট, সার্বিক স্বাস্থ্য ঘোষণাগুলি এবং ব্রাজিলে ভ্যাকসিনের প্রচার প্রক্রিয়ার পরিবেশ বিশ্লেষণ করা।

সিনোভ্যাক বায়োটেকের ভ্যাকসিন, যার নাম কোরোনাভ্যাক, ২০২১ সালের আগে থেকে ব্রাজিলে বিস্তৃত হয়েছে। এটি চীনের বাইরে প্রথম দেশগুলির মধ্যে একটি ছিল যা কোরোনাভ্যাক কে প্রাথমিক ভাবে সার্বিক ইমিউনাইজেশন প্রক্রিয়ার অংশ হিসাবে ব্যবহার করেছিল। কোরোনাভ্যাক কে ব্রাজিলে অনুমোদন দেওয়া হয় বুটান্টান ইনস্টিটিউট সহ সহযোগিতার মাধ্যমে ক্লিনিকাল পরীক্ষা পরিচালনার পর। যেমন সব ভ্যাকসিনের মতো কোরোনাভ্যাক কে স্বাস্থ্য ও প্রতিক্রিয়া সম্পর্কে সাংঘাতিক পরীক্ষা করা হয়েছিল স্বাস্থ্য কর্মী এবং সাধারণ জনগণের জন্য ব্যাপক প্রচারের আগে।

প্রাথমিক সামাজিক মাধ্যমে পোস্ট বলে যে পারাতি শহরে রেজিস্টার্ড কর্মীদের ভ্যাকসিন প্রাপ্ত হওয়ার পর তারা অস্বাস্থ্যকর প্রতিক্রিয়ার কারণে হাসপাতালে ভর্তি হয়েছেন। এই দাবি পরীক্ষা করতে আবশ্যক হয় ভ্যাকসিনের পরে ঘটে যাওয়া অস্বাস্থ্যকর ঘটনার প্রতিবেদন ব্যবস্থার বিষয়টি বুঝতে। ব্রাজিলের স্বাস্থ্য মন্ত্রণালয় এবং রাজ্য স্বাস্থ্য বিভাগ ভ্যাকসিন সম্পর্কিত যে কোনও গুরুতর ঘটনা যেমন ভর্তি হওয়া সম্পর্কে গুরুতর ঘটনা নিয়মিত পর্যবেক্ষণ এবং প্রকাশ করে। এগুলি প্রকাশ্যে প্রতিবেদন এবং সার্বিক স্বাস্থ্যের জন্য নিশ্চিত করার জন্য তদন্বিত করা হয়।

পারাতি শহরে বিস্তৃত ভ্যাকসিন প্রচারের সময় প্রতিবেদন এবং সংবাদপত্রের পরীক্ষা করে দেখা গেছে যে কোরোনাভ্যাক কারণে রেজিস্টার্ড কর্মীদের বা অন্যান্য স্বাস্থ্য কর্মীদের ভর্তি হওয়ার কোনও ছড়িয়ে পড়া কোনও প্রমাণ নেই। যদিও কোনও ব্যক্তি ভ্যাকসিন প্রাপ্ত হওয়ার পর ক্ষুধা বা মাথা ব্যথা বা মাংসপেশি ব্যথা এমন সামান্য প্রতিক্রিয়া সাধারণত ঘটে যায় কিন্তু গুরুতর প্রতিক্রিয়া কম। যে কোনও ব্যক্তি যার প্রতিক্রিয়া চিকিৎসার প্রয়োজন হয় তাদের ঘটনাগুলি তৎক্ষণাৎ তদন্বিত করা হয়। প্রাপ্ত রেকর্ড বার্ষিক পরিসংখ্যান বা ব্রাজিলে রিও ডি জেনেরিও এর অন্য কোনও স্থানে কোরোনাভ্যাক কারণে একটি কর্মী গ্রুপ ভর্তি হওয়ার কোনও প্রমাণ পাওয়া যায়নি।

যে কোনও সামাজিক মাধ্যমে ভ্যাকসিন প্রতিক্রিয়া সম্পর্কে ভুয়া তথ্য এবং গুজব সম্পর্কে প্রসারিত হয়েছিল। সামাজিক মাধ্যমে ভ্যাকসিনের উৎপত্তি নিয়ে সন্দেহ এবং বিশেষ করে চীনের কোম্পানি দ্বারা উত্পাদিত ভ্যাকসিন নিয়ে সন্দেহ জনিয়েছিল যা অনেক সময় অনুমান বা অতিরিক্ত দাবি প্রচারে অবদান রেখেছিল। স্বাস্থ্য কর্মকর্তারা সর্বদা কোরোনাভ্যাক এর সুরক্ষা প্রোফাইল বিষয়ে বলে যে এটি আন্তর্জাতিক স্তরে মান পূরণ করেছে এবং ব্রাজিলে কোভিড-১৯ হাসপাতালীকরণ এবং মৃত্যু হ্রাস করার জন্য অবদান রেখেছে।

সুতরাং পরিসংখ্যান এবং স্বীকৃত সংবাদপত্রে পারাতি শহরে রেজিস্টার্ড কর্মীদের কোরোনাভ্যাক ভ্যাকসিন প্রাপ্ত হওয়ার পর হাসপাতালে ভর্তি হওয়া দাবি কোনও প্রমাণ পাওয়া যায়নি। যদিও কোনও ভ্যাকসিন প্রতিক্রিয়া ঘটতে পারে, কিন্তু এই স্থানে স্বাস্থ্য কর্মীদের মধ্যে গুরুতর প্রতিক্রিয়া যে কোনও স্থানে বিনিময় করা হয়নি। সামাজিক মাধ্যমের ব্যবহারকারীদের কোনও বিশ্বস্ত উৎস থেকে ভ্যাকসিন তথ্য পরিচয় করার জন্য পরামর্শ দেওয়া হয় এবং প্রমাণিত নয় দাবি প্রচার করা থেকে বিরত থাকা উচিত যা সাধারণ ভুল বা ভয় সৃষ্টি করতে পারে।

In recent days, a social media post has gained attention by asserting that Jair Bolsonaro, former President of Brazil, disobeyed the Supreme Court and committed a crime of responsibility by ordering the sending of supplies and equipment to the state of Amazonas. The claim raises significant questions about presidential powers, legal boundaries, and the circumstances in which these actions took place.

To evaluate this claim, it is necessary to understand the context surrounding the federal government's response to crises in Amazonas, especially during Bolsonaro's administration. The state of Amazonas, and in particular its capital Manaus, faced severe challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, including a dramatic shortage of medical oxygen and other critical supplies in early 2021. The situation prompted widespread concern and urgent calls for federal intervention.

The Supreme Federal Court (STF) of Brazil played an active role during the pandemic, issuing decisions to clarify the responsibilities of federal, state, and municipal governments in handling the crisis. One of the key rulings by the STF was that governors and mayors retained autonomy to implement public health measures without interference from the federal government. However, the federal government retained its constitutional obligation to assist states in situations of calamity or emergency.

The social media claim suggests that Bolsonaro’s order to send supplies and equipment to Amazonas constituted a direct violation of a Supreme Court decision, and further, that this act was a "crime of responsibility"—a term used in Brazilian law to describe impeachable offenses committed by a president, such as violating constitutional duties or court orders.

Fact-checking this claim involves examining whether the Supreme Court explicitly prohibited the federal government from providing assistance to Amazonas, and whether Bolsonaro’s actions amounted to criminal misconduct. Available information indicates that while the STF emphasized the autonomy of local governments, it did not bar the federal government from offering support or sending resources during a public health emergency. In fact, the federal government is constitutionally mandated to support states facing disasters, provided such assistance does not override local decision-making.

Moreover, no public records or statements from the Supreme Court indicate that Bolsonaro was ordered not to send supplies or equipment to Amazonas. On the contrary, federal action to address the oxygen crisis was widely expected and, in many quarters, demanded. The notion that Bolsonaro committed a crime of responsibility by providing aid would require evidence of a clear, direct judicial order forbidding such assistance, which does not appear to exist.

It is important to note that Bolsonaro faced criticism over the federal response to the pandemic, including allegations of delays and inadequate support. However, the specific claim that he disobeyed the Supreme Court and committed a crime of responsibility by sending supplies to Amazonas does not align with the legal and factual record. While the federal government’s actions have been scrutinized for effectiveness and timeliness, providing emergency aid to a state in crisis falls within the president’s constitutional powers and duties.

In summary, there is no substantiated evidence that Jair Bolsonaro violated a Supreme Court order or committed a crime of responsibility by sending supplies and equipment to Amazonas. The claim, while reflecting ongoing political debate, is not supported by the facts surrounding the federal response to the crisis in Amazonas.

A recent social media post claims that Carlos Bolsonaro, son of former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro, skipped the vaccination line to receive a dose of the Covid-19 vaccine ahead of his eligibility. This claim has generated significant public interest due to the high-profile nature of the Bolsonaro family and the ongoing debates over equitable vaccine distribution in Brazil. In this fact-check, we examine the veracity of the claim and provide context on Brazil’s vaccination campaign.

**Background and Context**

Carlos Bolsonaro is a city councilman in Rio de Janeiro and the second son of Jair Bolsonaro, who was President of Brazil during the critical phases of the Covid-19 pandemic. The Bolsonaro administration attracted widespread criticism for its handling of public health guidelines and vaccine procurement. President Jair Bolsonaro himself was a vocal skeptic of Covid-19 vaccines for much of his term and publicly declared that he would not get vaccinated.

Brazil began its Covid-19 vaccination campaign in January 2021, with a strict priority system in place. Initial phases prioritized healthcare workers, the elderly, indigenous populations, and individuals with certain comorbidities. Vaccination was rolled out gradually, with each age group and priority category becoming eligible as more doses became available.

**Analysis of the Claim**

The core claim is that Carlos Bolsonaro received a vaccine dose before he was officially eligible, effectively skipping the line. To assess the accuracy of this statement, it is necessary to examine available records and reports regarding Carlos Bolsonaro’s vaccination status and the timeline for vaccine eligibility in Rio de Janeiro.

Public records indicate that Carlos Bolsonaro was born in December 1982, making him part of the 30-39 age group during the primary vaccine rollout. Official documents and statements from Rio de Janeiro’s municipal government show that this age group became eligible for vaccination in July 2021. There were extensive media reports and public scrutiny surrounding the vaccination of public officials, particularly those close to President Bolsonaro, due to concerns about preferential treatment.

Despite the rumors and the viral nature of the claim on social media, there is no credible evidence that Carlos Bolsonaro received a Covid-19 vaccine before his age group was eligible. In fact, Carlos Bolsonaro himself made public statements expressing skepticism about the vaccine, mirroring his father’s stance. There are no records or photographic evidence of him receiving the vaccine ahead of time, nor have any whistleblowers or municipal health officials corroborated the claim that he skipped the queue.

**Conclusion**

The claim that Carlos Bolsonaro skipped the line to receive a Covid-19 vaccine dose ahead of his eligibility is not supported by available evidence. Neither public records nor credible media reports indicate that he was vaccinated before his assigned turn. The Bolsonaro family’s public skepticism of the vaccine further undermines the likelihood of this scenario. While concerns about queue-jumping did arise elsewhere in Brazil, in this case, the claim about Carlos Bolsonaro appears to be unfounded.

A claim circulating on social media asserts that Covid-19 vaccines "alter the genetic code and can cause cancer." This statement has generated concern among some individuals and warrants a thorough examination using current scientific understanding and expert consensus.

To begin, it is important to clarify what is meant by "genetic code." The genetic code refers to the sequence of nucleotides in DNA that determines the instructions for building and maintaining an organism. Altering the genetic code would imply making permanent changes to an individual's DNA, a process known as genetic modification or gene editing.

Covid-19 vaccines approved for use in many countries are primarily of two types: messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines, such as those developed by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna, and viral vector vaccines, such as the Johnson & Johnson and AstraZeneca vaccines. Neither type has been shown to alter the recipient's DNA.

mRNA vaccines work by delivering a piece of genetic material (mRNA) into cells. This mRNA provides instructions for cells to produce a harmless spike protein found on the surface of the SARS-CoV-2 virus. The immune system recognizes this protein as foreign and mounts a response, preparing the body to fight off future infection. Importantly, mRNA does not integrate into or alter DNA. Human cells have mechanisms to prevent RNA from entering the nucleus, where DNA is housed, and the mRNA from the vaccine is rapidly broken down and removed by the body after it is used.

Viral vector vaccines use a harmless virus to deliver genetic material encoding the spike protein. This genetic material is also not integrated into the host’s DNA. The process is temporary, and the genetic instructions are not incorporated into the genome.

The second part of the claim suggests that Covid-19 vaccines can cause cancer. Cancer is a complex disease often resulting from mutations in DNA that lead to uncontrolled cell growth. To date, there is no evidence from clinical trials, surveillance, or epidemiological data indicating that Covid-19 vaccines cause cancer. The vaccines are designed to stimulate an immune response and do not contain substances known to induce cancer-causing mutations. Furthermore, the types of genetic material used in these vaccines do not persist in the body or interact with DNA in ways that would initiate cancer development.

Reports of adverse effects following vaccination have been closely monitored worldwide. While some side effects exist — such as temporary soreness, fever, or rare allergic reactions — there is no credible evidence linking Covid-19 vaccination to genetic alterations or cancer risk.

In summary, the claim that Covid-19 vaccines alter genetic code and cause cancer is not supported by scientific evidence. The vaccines do not modify DNA, and there is no indication they increase cancer risk. Misinformation of this nature can lead to vaccine hesitancy, undermining public health efforts to control the pandemic. It is important for individuals to seek information from trusted sources and consult healthcare professionals regarding vaccine safety.

पहिलो कुरा जाने आवश्यक छ कि "जेनेटिक कोड" के छ। जेनेटिक कोड जीव को निर्माण र रक्षा को निर्देशन को लागि डीएनए मा न्यूक्लिक एसिड को अनुक्रम हो। जेनेटिक कोड परिवर्तन एक व्यक्तिक डीएनए मा स्थायी परिवर्तन गर्ने बिचार गरिन्छ, जसलाई जेनेटिक म्युटेशन वा जीन एडिटिंग भनिन्छ।

केही देशहरूमा उपयोग अनुमोदित कोभिड-१९ टीका मुख्यतः दुई प्रकारका हुन्छन्: मेसेजर आरएनए (एमआरएनए) टीका, जस्तै प्फिजर-बायोन्टेक र मोडर्ना द्वारा विकसित टीका र भाइरल वेक्टर टीका, जस्तै जोनसन र जोनसन र एस्ट्राजेनेका टीका। यी दुई प्रकारका टीकाहरू बाट ग्राहकको डीएनए परिवर्तन भएको छैन।

एमआरएनए टीकाहरू आफ्नो सेलमा एक भाग जेनेटिक सामग्री (एमआरएनए) लाई प्रसारित गर्दछ। यो एमआरएनए सेलहरूलाई सार्स-कोभ-२ भाइरसको सतहमा पाइ रहेको एक असुरक्षित टिप प्रोटीन बनाउन निर्देशन दिन्छ। इम्यून सिस्टम यो प्रोटीनलाई विदेशी भन्दै चिन्छ र अनुक्रमित चिन्ता गर्दछ, जुन भाइरस आक्रमणको विरुद्ध शरीरलाई तयार गर्दछ। महत्वपूर्ण रूपमा, एमआरएनए डीएनए मा समावेश गर्दैन वा डीएनए परिवर्तन गर्दैन। मानव सेलहरू एरआरएनएलाई नाभिकमा जहाँ डीएनए रहेछ अन्तर्गत आउन रोक्छ र टीका एमआरएनए को उपयोग पछि शरीरले त्वरित रूपमा विघटित र बर्बाद गर्दछ।

भाइरल वेक्टर टीकाहरू एक असुरक्षित भाइरसलाई प्रयोग गरेर स्पाइक प्रोटीनको जेनेटिक सामग्री समावेश गर्दछ। यो जेनेटिक सामग्री विशेष रूपमा डिजाइन गरिएको छ र यो भोजकको डीएनए मा समावेश गर्दैन। प्रक्रिया स्थायी छ र जेनेटिक निर्देशन जीनोम मा समावेश गर्दैन।

दावीको दुई भाग भन्छ कि कोभिड-१९ टीका क्यान्सर उत्पन्न गर्छ। क्यान्सर एक जटिल रोग हो जुन डीएनए मा विकृतिहरू द्वारा अपरिचित सेल विस्तार गर्ने परिणाम हो। अब तक क्लिनिकल ट्राइल, सर्भिस र एपिडेमियोलोजिकल डेटामा कोभिड-१९ टीका क्यान्सर उत्पन्न गर्ने कुनै प्रमाण छैन। टीकाहरू इम्यून रेस्पोन्स उत्प्रेरण गर्न डिज़ाइन गरिएका छन् र यी टीकाहरूमा क्यान्सर उत्पन्न गर्ने विकृतिहरूको बारेमा ज्ञात अवस्थाहरू छैन। यी टीकाहरूमा प्रयोग गरिएका जेनेटिक सामग्रीहरू शरीरमा लामो समय रहेको छैन वा डीएनए र अन्य रूपमा क्यान्सर विकास शुरु गर्ने तरल प्रभाव छैन।

टीका प्राप्ति पछि बुरात असरहरू वैश्विक रूपमा निगरानी गरिएको छ। केही असरहरू छन् - जस्तै अस्थायी चोट, ज्वर, वा बेहद दुर्लभ अलर्जी असर - कोभिड-१९ टीका लगाउँदा जेनेटिक परिवर्तन वा क्यान्सर जोखिम जोडिएको कुनै विश्वसनीय प्रमाण छैन।

सारांशमा, कोभिड-१९ टीका जेनेटिक कोड परिवर्तन र क्यान्सर उत्पन्न गर्ने दावी वैज्ञानिक प्रमाण द्वारा समर्थित छैन। टीकाहरू डीएनए परिवर्तन गर्दैन र यी टीकाहरू जेनेटिक परिवर्तन वा क्यान्सर जोखिम बढाउँदैन। यै विचार विश्वास नगरे भए टीका लगाउँदा विश्वास नगरे भए जनता को लागि प्रमुख स्वास्थ्य अभियान असफल हुन सक्छ। व्यक्तिहरू जानकारी के छ भन्नकर विश्वास गर्न योग्य स्रोतहरू खोज्नु आवश्यक छ र टीका सुरक्षा बारे चिकित्सकहरूको परामर्श लिनु आवश्यक छ।
article_summary: A afirmação de que vacinas contra a Covid-19 alteram o código genético e causam câncer é falsa, segundo a ciência. Vacinas de mRNA e vetores virais não modificam o DNA, pois o material genético delas não se integra ao genoma humano. Não há evidências de que as vacinas aumentem o risco de câncer, e efeitos adversos relatados não estão ligados a alterações genéticas.

In early 2021, Brazil faced one of its worst public health crises during the COVID-19 pandemic. The state of Amazonas, particularly its capital Manaus, suffered a dramatic shortage of medical oxygen, leading to tragic scenes in hospitals and widespread international concern. Amid this crisis, numerous private individuals and businesses stepped forward to assist, drawing significant attention on social media and in the press. Among the names frequently mentioned was Luciano Hang, a businessman known for his support of former President Jair Bolsonaro and for his outspoken political stances.

The social media post under scrutiny claims: "Luciano Hang, Bolsonaro's militant businessman, donated 200 oxygen cylinders to the state of Amazonas." To verify this statement, it is essential to understand the context, review Hang's actions during the crisis, and assess the accuracy of the specifics in the claim.

Luciano Hang is the founder and owner of Havan, one of Brazil's largest department store chains. Hang has gained notoriety not only for his business acumen but also for his vocal support of Jair Bolsonaro. His political activity has often made headlines, sometimes overshadowing his business ventures. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Hang and Havan were involved in several charitable initiatives, including donations of medical supplies.

The shortage of oxygen in Manaus became critical in January 2021, with hospitals unable to supply enough oxygen to patients suffering from severe COVID-19 symptoms. Reports flooded the media showing desperate relatives searching for oxygen tanks on the black market, and health professionals crying out for help. In response, a range of private companies, NGOs, and individuals mobilized resources to alleviate the crisis.

According to statements from Havan and media coverage at the time, Luciano Hang did indeed participate in relief efforts. Hang announced publicly, both through Havan's channels and his personal social media, that he had arranged the donation of oxygen cylinders to Amazonas. The number cited in most public communications was 200 cylinders, matching the claim in the social media post. Hang stated that the cylinders were purchased and sent by Havan to be distributed in hospitals in need throughout Manaus and surrounding areas.

While there were some discussions about the logistics and speed of delivery, there is no substantial evidence contradicting the core of the claim. The local government of Amazonas acknowledged the receipt of donations from several private entities, including Havan. News reports at the time confirmed that trucks carrying oxygen cylinders donated by Havan arrived in Manaus, and images of the delivery circulated widely.

In summary, the social media post accurately reflects the actions taken by Luciano Hang during the oxygen crisis in Amazonas. Hang, widely recognized as a staunch supporter of Bolsonaro, did donate 200 oxygen cylinders to the state at a time of acute need. The donation was part of a broader mobilization of private support for the region. While Hang’s political affiliations often color public perceptions of his actions, the facts support the central claim: Luciano Hang, through Havan, provided significant material assistance to Amazonas during one of its darkest moments in the COVID-19 pandemic.

In recent days, a social media post has circulated claiming that the Governor of São Paulo decreed isolation measures for the state and then traveled to the neighboring state of Rio de Janeiro the following weekend. This claim has sparked debate regarding the governor’s adherence to public health guidelines and generated criticism from some users who accuse the governor of double standards. This article examines the accuracy of the claim and provides necessary context to understand the situation.

To begin, it is important to clarify the timeline and content of the alleged isolation measures. Governors in Brazil, including the Governor of São Paulo, have the authority to implement public health directives, such as social distancing, closure of non-essential businesses, and restrictions on gatherings, especially during times of increased COVID-19 transmission. These measures are typically announced in response to rising case numbers or new variants, with the intention of reducing the spread of the virus and protecting the healthcare system.

According to official statements, the Governor of São Paulo did issue isolation measures during the specified period. These measures included limiting the capacity of restaurants and bars, reducing the hours of operation for non-essential services, and urging residents to remain at home unless travel was necessary. The governor emphasized the importance of these restrictions in curbing the spread of COVID-19 and repeatedly called for public cooperation.

The second element of the claim alleges that the governor then traveled to Rio de Janeiro the following weekend. Based on publicly available information, including news reports and social media activity, the governor was indeed seen in Rio de Janeiro during this timeframe. The reason for the trip, according to official sources, was participation in a private family event. Photographs of the governor in Rio de Janeiro surfaced online, fueling public scrutiny and questioning the consistency between the governor’s actions and the directives given to São Paulo residents.

Fact-checking this claim, all key elements are confirmed: the governor did establish isolation measures and subsequently traveled to Rio de Janeiro the next weekend. However, it is important to contextualize the situation. The isolation measures applied to the state of São Paulo and were not legally binding for the neighboring state of Rio de Janeiro. The governor’s trip did not technically violate any laws, and there is no evidence that the governor failed to follow public health guidelines while in Rio de Janeiro. Nevertheless, the optics of the situation have raised concerns among constituents, who argue that leaders should set an example by limiting non-essential travel, especially immediately after implementing restrictions.

In summary, the social media post’s core claim is accurate: the Governor of São Paulo implemented isolation measures for the state and traveled to Rio de Janeiro the following weekend. While the governor’s actions did not break any regulations, the incident underscores the importance of public officials modeling the behavior they ask of citizens. Public trust can be affected when there is a perceived gap between official directives and personal conduct, highlighting the complex relationship between leadership, responsibility, and public perception during times of crisis.

A claim circulating on social media states that President Joe Biden said chloroquine is effective against Covid-19. This assertion has attracted significant attention, given the ongoing debates around treatments for Covid-19 and the role of political figures in shaping public health messages. This article examines the veracity of the claim, putting it into the context of public statements by Joe Biden, the scientific community’s position on chloroquine, and the broader discussion about Covid-19 treatment recommendations.

Chloroquine, and its derivative hydroxychloroquine, are medications long used to treat malaria and certain autoimmune diseases. Early in the Covid-19 pandemic, there was considerable interest in chloroquine as a potential treatment for the novel coronavirus. Some preliminary laboratory studies suggested possible antiviral effects, and anecdotal reports fueled enthusiasm for its use. However, as more rigorous clinical trials were conducted, the evidence increasingly showed that chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine were not effective in preventing or treating Covid-19. Major health authorities, including the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the World Health Organization, ultimately advised against the use of these drugs outside of clinical trials due to lack of efficacy and potential side effects.

The claim that President Joe Biden said chloroquine is effective against Covid-19 merits close scrutiny. As of June 2024, there is no record of Joe Biden, either as a candidate or as President, publicly stating that chloroquine is effective against Covid-19. Throughout his presidential campaign and subsequent administration, Biden’s approach to Covid-19 has consistently emphasized reliance on scientific expertise and guidance from federal health agencies. His public statements have focused on promoting vaccination, mask-wearing, and other evidence-based interventions rather than unproven pharmaceuticals.

In contrast, the discussion about chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine was more prominent during the previous administration, when some officials, including former President Donald Trump, publicly advocated for their use. These endorsements were widely scrutinized and sometimes contradicted by health authorities. Biden, by comparison, has refrained from making unsupported claims about treatments, instead urging Americans to follow the advice of medical professionals and regulatory agencies.

Fact-checking the core claim reveals it to be false. There are no speeches, interviews, press releases, or official documents in which Joe Biden claims chloroquine is effective against Covid-19. Any suggestion to the contrary appears to be a misattribution or a distortion of public discourse surrounding Covid-19 treatments. Misinformation about Covid-19 therapies has been a persistent challenge throughout the pandemic, and attributing unsupported claims to high-profile figures can contribute to public confusion and undermine trust in health recommendations.

In summary, President Joe Biden has not publicly stated that chloroquine is effective against Covid-19. The scientific consensus remains that chloroquine is not a recommended treatment for the disease. Social media users are encouraged to seek information from credible sources and exercise caution when encountering claims about Covid-19 treatments attributed to political leaders.
