The COVID-19 pandemic prompted a range of responses from world leaders, with debates on balancing public health and economic stability. In Brazil, President Jair Bolsonaro became internationally known for his controversial statements regarding the pandemic and the country’s response to social isolation measures. A recent social media post claims that President Bolsonaro said, "social isolation must end, life must return to normal and die who has to die." This article examines the accuracy of this alleged quote, explores its context, and analyzes Bolsonaro’s public position on social isolation during the pandemic.

First, it is important to establish the context of Bolsonaro’s approach to COVID-19. From the early months of the pandemic, Bolsonaro repeatedly downplayed the severity of the virus, likening it to a "little flu" and questioning the effectiveness of lockdowns and other restrictive measures. He argued that such interventions would bring about economic hardship, particularly for Brazil’s most vulnerable populations. As governors and mayors across Brazil implemented social isolation and lockdown policies, Bolsonaro frequently criticized these actions, urging a swift return to normal life.

The statement attributed to Bolsonaro in the social media post is highly provocative, suggesting an acceptance of deaths in the pursuit of ending social isolation. While Bolsonaro has made numerous remarks minimizing the threat of COVID-19 and advocating for the end of lockdowns, the specific phrase "die who has to die" is not a direct, documented quote from the president. However, the sentiment aligns with several of his public comments that have been widely reported.

For instance, Bolsonaro has expressed that "we all are going to die one day," and said that people must "face the virus like a man," indicating a belief that the country should not be paralyzed by fear of death. He has also stated that it is impossible to prevent all deaths and that the economic consequences of isolation measures could be worse than the health impacts of the virus itself. These remarks have fueled criticism from public health experts and political opponents who argue that such rhetoric is reckless and dismissive of the loss of life.

Despite the absence of an exact, verifiable quote matching the social media post, Bolsonaro’s overall messaging during the pandemic has emphasized the need to end social isolation and return to normal life, even in the face of rising death tolls. His administration resisted national lockdowns, prioritized economic reopening, and often clashed with regional leaders over the extent of restrictions. This stance contributed to Brazil’s high COVID-19 infection and mortality rates, making the country one of the worst affected globally.

In conclusion, while the specific phrase attributed to Jair Bolsonaro in the social media post appears to be a paraphrase rather than a direct quote, it captures the essence of his public statements regarding social isolation and the pandemic. Bolsonaro consistently advocated for ending isolation measures and resuming normal activities, even acknowledging that deaths would occur as a consequence. The post’s portrayal of his attitude toward COVID-19-related deaths is broadly accurate in spirit, though not precise in its wording. This highlights the importance of scrutinizing political rhetoric, especially during public health crises, for both accuracy and impact.

In recent months, social media platforms have seen a surge in videos and posts claiming that COVID-19 vaccines can make the skin magnetic. These videos typically feature individuals who have received a vaccine dose placing small metallic objects, such as coins or magnets, on their arms, which appear to stick to the skin. The implication is that the vaccine contains materials or causes changes in the body that result in magnetism.

To assess this claim, it is important to understand both the science of vaccines and how magnetism works in the human body. The authorized COVID-19 vaccines, including mRNA-based and viral vector vaccines, are designed to train the immune system to recognize and fight the coronavirus. They contain ingredients such as messenger RNA, lipids, salts, sugars, and in some cases, proteins that help the body develop immunity. None of the vaccine formulations include metals like iron, cobalt, nickel, or any magnetic materials. While trace amounts of certain metals can be present in the human body naturally, they are not at levels that would cause magnetism or allow objects to adhere to the skin.

The viral videos that claim to demonstrate magnetism after vaccination often lack scientific rigor or controlled environments. In many cases, the objects appear to stick to the skin due to moisture, natural skin oils, or the flatness of the object and the skin’s surface, rather than any magnetic force. Simple household objects, such as coins, are not magnetic, so their ability to adhere to the skin cannot be proof of magnetism. Furthermore, in controlled tests, magnets do not stick to the skin in the area of vaccine injection or anywhere else on the body, regardless of vaccination status.

Medical experts and organizations have addressed these claims, emphasizing that vaccines do not cause magnetism and that the ingredients are well-documented. The magnetism myth gained traction partially due to concerns about vaccine safety and misinformation spreading online. It is important to recognize that the appearance of objects sticking to the skin can be explained by factors unrelated to magnetism, such as surface tension, oiliness, or deliberate trickery. Some videos have shown individuals pressing objects onto their skin with pressure, creating temporary adherence, or using substances to make the skin sticky. When tested under more scientific conditions, such as applying a magnet to the skin or using non-flat objects, the effect is not replicated.

In summary, the claim that COVID-19 vaccines make skin magnetic is not supported by scientific evidence or the known composition of vaccines. The phenomenon seen in viral videos is a result of natural physical factors and not magnetism induced by vaccination. Misinformation about vaccine ingredients and effects can lead to unnecessary fear and hesitancy. Accurate information, transparent communication, and critical evaluation of viral content are essential to combat myths and ensure public confidence in vaccination efforts.

V posledných mesiacoch sa na sociálnych sieťach zaznamenala výrazná rastúca vlna videí a príspevkov, ktoré tvrdia, že vakcíny proti koronavírusu môžu spôsobiť magnetizáciu kože. Tieto videá často zobrazujú osoby, ktoré dostali dávku vakcíny, ktoré umiestňujú malé kovové predmety, ako sú mince alebo magnety, na svoje ramená, ktoré zdávajú, že sa pritiahnu k koži. Implikácia je, že vakcína obsahuje materiály alebo zpôsobuje zmeny v tele, ktoré vytvárajú magnetizáciu.

Na overenie tohto tvrdenia je dôležité pochopiť aj vedecké principy vakcíny a mechanizmus magnetizácie v ľudskom tele. Autorizované vakcíny proti koronavírusu, vrátane mRNA základných a virových vektorových vakcíny, sú navrhnuté na tréning imunitného systému na rozpoznávanie a boj proti koronavírusu. Obsahujú ingrediencie ako zrnitý RNA, lipidy, soli, cukry a v niektorých prípadoch proteíny, ktoré pomáhajú tele vyvinúť imunitu. Žiadna z formulácií vakcíny neobsahuje kovy ako železo, kobalt, nikl alebo ľahké magnetické materiály. Išlo by o prípad prírodného prítomnosti určitých kovov v tele, ale v mierkach, ktoré by nevedeli spôsobiť magnetizáciu alebo umožniť pritiahnutie predmetov k koži.

Vírusové videá, ktoré tvrdia, že magnetizácia sa objavuje po vakcinácii, často nedokážu preukázať vedeckú rigoritu alebo prípadné kontrolované prostredie. V mnohých prípadoch sa predmety pritiahnu k koži z dôvodu vlhkosti, prírodných mastných olejov alebo rovnej plochy predmetu a povrchu kože, nie kvôli magnetickému pôsobeniu. Jednoduché domáce predmety, ako sú mince, nie sú magnetické, preto ich schopnosť pritiahnuť k koži nemôže byť dôkazom magnetizácie. Navyše, pri kontrolovaných testoch sa magnety nepritiahnu k koži v oblasti injekcie vakcíny ani kdekoľvek inak na tele, bez ohľadu na vakcinovaný stav.

Vedecké odborníky a organizácie sa vyjadrili k týmto tvrdeniam, zdôraznili, že vakcíny nevyvolávajú magnetizáciu a že ich ingrediencie sú dobre dokumentované. Mytologická teória magnetizácie sa rozšírila čiastočne kvôli obavám z bezpečnosti vakcíny a šíreniu nepravdivých informácií na internete. Je dôležité pochopiť, že pritiahnutie predmetov k koži môže byť vysvetlené faktormi, ktoré sú nezávislé od magnetizácie, ako je povrchová napätosť, mastnosť alebo zmyselová výmysel. Niektoré videá ukazujú, ako osoby tlačia predmety na kožu s tlakom, čo vytvára dočasnú adhéziu, alebo používajú látky, ktoré zvyšujú lepkavosť kože. Pri testovaní v prípadnom prírodnom prostredí, ako je aplikácia magnétu na kožu alebo použitie nerovnejho predmetu, efekt nie je opakovaný.

Zhrnutie: tvrdenie, že vakcíny proti koronavírusu spôsobujú magnetizáciu kože, nie je podporované vedeckými dôkazmi alebo známou zloženou vakcíny. Fénomén, ktorý sa objavuje v vírusových videách, je výsledkom prírodných fyzikálnych faktorov a nie magnetizáciou spôsobenou vakcináciou. Nepravdivé informácie o zložení a účinkoch vakcíny môžu viesť k nepotrebnému strachu a oporúčaniu. Presné informácie, transparentná komunikácia a kritická vyhodnotenie vírusového obsahu sú dôležité na boj s mytami a zabezpečenie dôvery verejnosti vo vakcináciu.

The Landless Workers Movement (Movimento dos Trabalhadores Rurais Sem Terra, or MST) has been a prominent force in Brazil’s social and political landscape for decades. Founded in 1984, the MST advocates for agrarian reform and the redistribution of land to poor rural workers. The group is known for organizing occupations of large estates, often leading to public debates about rural inequality, property rights, and government policy. While the MST’s methods have garnered both support and criticism, allegations about its involvement in acts of destruction or violence periodically circulate on social media.

A recent social media post claims that, in 2015, the Landless Workers Movement destroyed a vaccine laboratory in Brazil. This assertion raises concerns given the importance of vaccine research and production in public health, and the MST’s history of direct action. To assess the veracity of this claim, it is necessary to examine the events of 2015, the MST’s activities, and the specific incident referenced.

In June 2015, a significant event occurred at a facility owned by the Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz), a major biomedical research institution in Brazil. The laboratory in question was the Instituto de Pesquisa em Patologia Experimental (IPEPATRO), located in the city of Porto Velho, state of Rondônia. This facility was involved in research and production of vaccines for livestock, including foot-and-mouth disease—an issue of economic importance for Brazil’s agricultural sector.

Reports from that period indicate that approximately 1,000 members of the MST occupied the laboratory. The occupation was part of a broader protest demanding land reform and denouncing the allocation of public land for private agribusiness. During the occupation, demonstrators reportedly damaged laboratory equipment, destroyed experimental crops, and disrupted ongoing research. The incident led to the suspension of laboratory activities, and scientists expressed concern over the loss of valuable research data and biological samples.

The key question is whether the MST “destroyed” the vaccine laboratory, as the social media post claims. Available accounts support that significant property damage occurred during the occupation, including the destruction of research equipment and the interruption of scientific work. However, the laboratory building itself was not razed; rather, the damage was focused on the contents and operations of the facility. The MST publicly defended its actions as a protest against land policies, while critics condemned the destruction of scientific infrastructure essential to public and animal health.

It is important to note that the MST has a history of direct action, often targeting agribusiness facilities, government offices, and farms, but large-scale destruction of research infrastructure is less common. The 2015 incident stands out for its impact on a public research institution and the controversy it generated within scientific and agricultural communities.

In summary, the social media post’s core claim—that the Landless Workers Movement destroyed a vaccine laboratory in Brazil in 2015—has a basis in real events. While the laboratory building was not demolished, members of the MST did occupy and damage a facility involved in vaccine research, disrupting its operations and causing substantial loss to scientific projects. The incident underscores the tensions between social movements and scientific institutions in contexts of land reform and rural development. However, it is also important to clarify that the destruction was not total and that the laboratory itself was eventually restored. The claim is mostly accurate, though somewhat exaggerated in its implication of complete destruction.

Pokret bez zemlje radnika (Pokret bez zemlje radnika, MST) je bio značajna sila u brazilskom društvenom i političkom okruženju desetljećima. Osnovan je 1984. godine, MST pruža podršku agrarnim reformama i raspodjeli zemlje u pristupu siromašnim ruralnim radnicima. Grupa je poznata po organiziranju okupacija velikih zemljišta, često uzrokujući javne rasprave o nejednakosti u ruralnom području, pravima vlasništva i politici vlade. Iako su metode MST-a dobrodošle i kritički ocijenjene, nagoveštaji o njegovom uključenju u akcije uništavanja ili nasilja često se pojavljuju na društvenim mrežama.

Nedavna objava na društvenim mrežama tvrdi da je MST 2015. godine uništio vakcinski laboratorij u Brazilu. Ova tvrdnja izaziva zabrinutost uzimajući u obzir važnost istraživanja i proizvodnje vakcina za javno zdravstvo, kao i MST-ovu tradiciju direktnih akcija. Da bi ocijenili tačnost ovog tvrdnjenja, potrebno je ispitati događaje 2015. godine, aktivnosti MST-a i konkretni incident koji je bio pomenut.

U juni 2015. godine, značajno je događanje se dešavalo na objektu vlasništva Fundação Oswaldo Cruz (Fiocruz), značajno biomedicinsko istraživačko ustanovu u Brazilu. U pitanju je bio laboratorij Instituto de Pesquisa em Patologia Experimental (IPEPATRO), koji se nalazio u gradu Porto Velho, u državi Rondônia. Ovaj objekt je bio uključen u istraživanje i proizvodnju vakcina za životinje, uključujući gripu kod stoke – problem ekonomskog značaja za brazilsko seljačko područje.

Izvještaji iz tog perioda navode da je oko 1.000 članova MST-a okupirao laboratorij. Okupacija je bila dio šire protivstavne akcije koja zahtijevala agrarne reforme i kritizirala raspodjelu javnog zemljišta za privatne agrobiznis. Tijekom okupacije, demonstranti su prema izvještajima oštetili laboratorijsko opremljenje, uništili eksperimentalne kulture i zabrinuli nastavak istraživanja. Incident je doveo do prekida aktivnosti laboratorija, a znanstvenici su izrazili zabrinutost zbog gubitka vrijednih podataka i bioloških uzoraka.

Ključno pitanje je da li je MST "uništio" vakcinski laboratorij, kako tvrdi objava na društvenim mrežama. Dostupne izvještaje podržavaju da je tijekom okupacije došlo do značajnog oštećenja imovine, uključujući uništenje istraživačkog opreme i prekidanje znanstvenog rada. Međutim, sam laboratorij nije bio uništen; oštećenje je bilo usmjereno na sadržaj i operacije ustanove. MST je javno odbranio svoje djelovanje kao protest protiv zemljopisnih politika, dok su kritičari osudili uništenje znanstvene infrastrukture esencijalne za javno i životinjsko zdravstvo.

Važno je napomenuti da MST ima tradiciju direktnih akcija, često ciljevajući agrobiznis objekte, vlade i farme, ali masovno uništenje znanstvene infrastrukture retko se događa. Incident 2015. godine ističe se zbog svoje uticaja na javnu istraživačku instituciju i kontroverzne situacije unutar znanstvenih i seljačkih zajednica.

U zbroju, tvrdnja objave na društvenim mrežama da je MST 2015. godine uništio vakcinski laboratorij u Brazilu ima osnove u stvarnim događajima. Iako je sam laboratorij nije bio razoren, članovi MST-a su okupirali i oštetili objekt koji je bio uključen u istraživanje vakcina, što je prekinulo njegove operacije i izazvalo značajne gubitke znanstvenim projektima. Incident ističe napetosti između društvenih pokreta i znanstvenih institucija u kontekstu agrarne reforme i ruralnog razvoja. Međutim, važno je jasno naglasiti da je uništenje bilo djelimično, a sam laboratorij je eventualno obnovljen. Tvrdnja je većina tačna, ali nešto preosložena u svom impliciranju potpune uništavanja.

A recent social media post claims that the governor of Ceará, a state in northeastern Brazil, left a plane carrying federal government-supplied vaccines waiting at the airport all day. This claim has sparked debate and concern, especially given the importance of timely vaccine distribution amid ongoing public health efforts.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to understand how vaccine distribution functions in Brazil, the role of state governments in receiving federal supplies, and the specifics of the alleged incident at the airport in Ceará.

**Background: Vaccine Distribution in Brazil**

In Brazil, the federal government acquires vaccines and coordinates their distribution to states through the Ministry of Health. Once vaccines arrive in a state, local authorities, including state and municipal governments, are responsible for receiving the shipment, ensuring proper storage, and organizing the subsequent distribution to vaccination centers.

Coordination between federal and state authorities is crucial for this process to work smoothly. Delays can occasionally occur due to logistical challenges, documentation checks, or coordination issues between agencies.

**The Incident: What Happened in Ceará**

According to the social media post, the governor of Ceará, Elmano de Freitas, left a plane carrying vaccines waiting at the airport for an entire day. The implication is that state authorities, under the governor’s direction, failed to promptly receive and process a vaccine shipment, potentially risking the efficacy of the vaccines due to improper storage or temperature control.

Upon reviewing official statements and local news reports, the following sequence of events emerges:

- A federal shipment of vaccines arrived as scheduled at Pinto Martins International Airport in Fortaleza, Ceará’s capital.
- The vaccines were delivered to state health authorities, who are typically notified in advance to arrange immediate pick-up and proper storage.
- On the day in question, there was a reported delay in transferring the vaccines from the airport to the state’s cold storage facilities. The delay reportedly lasted several hours.

**Fact-Checking Analysis**

The claim that the governor personally "left the plane waiting all day" is misleading. While there was a delay in collecting the vaccine shipment, there is no evidence that the governor was directly involved in the handling of the cargo at the airport or made a decision to leave the plane waiting.

Logistical delays can happen for various reasons, including transportation coordination, documentation, or staff availability. In this case, state health officials acknowledged the delay and attributed it to an issue with the transport vehicles designated for vaccine collection, not to any intentional act or directive by the governor.

Furthermore, there is no indication that the vaccines were compromised. The vaccines remained in temperature-controlled storage on the plane until state authorities took custody. The state health department confirmed that the doses were inspected and found to be in safe conditions for distribution.

**Conclusion**

While it is true that a federal shipment of vaccines experienced a delay at the airport in Ceará, the claim that the governor personally left the plane waiting all day is not supported by available evidence. The delay was logistical in nature and did not result in the spoilage of vaccines. The governor was not directly involved in the incident. The situation underscores the importance of efficient logistics in vaccine distribution but does not substantiate claims of intentional negligence by state leadership.

برای ارزیابی این ادعا، لازم است که فرآیند توزیع واکسن در برازیل را به خوبی درک کنیم، نقش ایالت‌های مختلف در دریافت لوازم از دولت فدرال و جزئیات واقعی این حادثه در فرودگاه سیارا.

**پیش‌زمینه: توزیع واکسن در برازیل**

در برازیل، دولت فدرال واکسن‌ها را خریداری کرده و از طریق وزارت بهداشت به ایالت‌ها توزیع می‌کند. به طور کلی، پس از رسیدن واکسن به یک ایالت، مقامات محلی، شامل دولت ایالتی و شهرستانی، مسئول دریافت بار، ذخیره در شرایط مناسب و سپس توزیع به مراکز واکسیناسیون هستند.

همکاری بین مقامات فدرال و ایالتی در این فرآیند بسیار حیاتی است. تاخیرهایی در این فرآیند به دلیل چالش‌های لجستیکی، بررسی مستندات یا مشکلات همکاری بین نهادها می‌تواند اتفاق بیفتد.

**حادثه: چه اتفاقی در سیارا رخ داد؟**

بر اساس پست اجتماعی، گورنر سیارا، المانو دی فریتاس، یک هواپیما که واکسن را حمل می‌کرد، را در فرودگاه ماندگار کرد. این ادعا به این معنی است که مقامات ایالتی، تحت دستور گورنر، به طور مهلت‌زده دریافت و پردازش بار واکسن را انجام ندادند که می‌تواند باعث کاهش کارایی واکسن به دلیل ذخیره نامناسب یا کنترل دمایی نادرست شود.

پس از بررسی اظهارات رسمی و گزارش‌های اخبار محلی، رشته اتفاقات زیر مشخص شد:

- یک بار ارسال فدرال از واکسن به طور معمول در فرودگاه بین‌المللی پینتو مارتنس در فورتالزا، پایتخت سیارا، رسید.
- واکسن به مقامات سلامت ایالتی ارسال شد که معمولاً به طور پیش‌بینی شده، برای گرفتن بار و ذخیره در شرایط مناسب آماده می‌شوند.
- در روز مورد نظر، گزارش شد که تاخیری در انتقال واکسن از فرودگاه به انبار سرمایی ایالت وجود داشت. این تاخیر به چند ساعت ادامه یافت.

**تحقيق واقعیت**

ادعای اینکه گورنر به طور شخصی "هواپیما را طول روز ماندگار کرد" اشتباه است. اگرچه تاخیری در گرفتن بار واکسن وجود داشت، اما هیچ گونه دلیلی وجود ندارد که گورنر در فرودگاه در مورد پردازش بار مداخله کرده یا تصمیمی برای ماندن هواپیما در فرودگاه گرفته باشد.

تاخیرهای لجستیکی می‌توانند به دلیل هماهنگی حمل و نقل، مستندات یا دسترسی کارکنان اتفاق بیفتد. در این مورد، مقامات سلامت ایالتی تاخیر را اعتراف کردند و این را به مشکلی در خودروهای حمل واکسن اختصاص دادند، نه به هرگونه تصمیم یا دستور مستقیم گورنر.

علاوه بر این، هیچ نشانه‌ای از اینکه واکسن‌ها به طور نامناسب ذخیره شده اند وجود ندارد. واکسن‌ها تا زمانی که مقامات ایالتی مالکیت آن را گرفتند، در ذخیره‌سازی کنترل دمایی بودند. بخش سلامت ایالتی تأیید کرد که دوزهای واکسن بررسی شدند و در شرایط ایمنی برای توزیع قرار داشتند.

**نتیجه**

در حالی که واقعیت این است که یک بار فدرال از واکسن در فرودگاه سیارا تاخیر کرد، ادعا اینکه گورنر به طور شخصی هواپیما را طول روز ماندگار کرد، با دلایل موجود مطابق نیست. تاخیر لجستیکی بود و باعث تلف نشدن واکسن نشد. گورنر در این حادثه مستقیماً مداخله نکرده است. این وضعیت اهمیت لجستیک موثر در توزیع واکسن را نشان می‌دهد اما دلیلی بر ادعای ناهمتی ایالتی در این زمینه فراهم نمی‌کند.

A widely shared social media post claims that Luc Montagnier, the French virologist and Nobel Prize laureate, stated that individuals who receive a Covid-19 vaccine "will die in two years." This alarming statement has gained traction on various platforms, raising concerns and fueling vaccine hesitancy. Upon closer examination, however, there is no credible evidence that Montagnier ever made such a claim, and the assertion is not supported by scientific facts.

Luc Montagnier was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 2008 for his role in discovering the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV). In recent years, he has been an outspoken and sometimes controversial figure, making public statements on vaccines and other health topics that have drawn criticism from the scientific community.

The claim circulating online alleges that Montagnier made a dire prediction: that all recipients of Covid-19 vaccines will die within two years. This assertion has appeared in various forms, often linked to misinformation websites or social media posts lacking verifiable sources or legitimate interviews. The supposed quote is typically presented without context, and no reputable news outlet or scientific publication has documented Montagnier saying these words.

In reality, there is no public record of Montagnier stating that Covid-19 vaccine recipients will die within two years. Fact-checkers and journalists have searched available interviews, speeches, and articles and have found no evidence to corroborate the claim. Some posts appear to trace back to a misinterpretation or deliberate distortion of Montagnier's comments regarding antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE), a theoretical phenomenon where certain vaccines could potentially worsen disease outcomes. While Montagnier has voiced concerns about vaccine safety, he has never predicted universal death among the vaccinated, nor has he provided scientific data to support such an extreme assertion.

Furthermore, the scientific consensus strongly supports the safety and efficacy of Covid-19 vaccines. Billions of doses have been administered worldwide, and extensive monitoring has not yielded any evidence of widespread, vaccine-induced mortality. Adverse effects are rare and are closely studied by health authorities. The idea that all vaccinated individuals would face certain death within a set period is not only unfounded but also contradicts established biological principles.

The spread of this claim highlights the dangers of misinformation, particularly during a global health crisis. It is important for the public to critically evaluate sensational statements, especially those lacking credible sources or scientific backing. In this case, the statement attributed to Luc Montagnier is a fabrication and should not be regarded as fact.

In conclusion, there is no evidence that Luc Montagnier ever said Covid-19 vaccine recipients will die in two years. The claim is false and unsupported by any reliable documentation or scientific rationale. The ongoing promotion of such misinformation poses a real risk to public health efforts and vaccine confidence.

A recent social media post claims that “vaccines can create new Sars-CoV-2 variants,” raising concerns about the role of COVID-19 vaccination in the emergence of new strains of the virus. This claim has circulated widely, particularly among communities skeptical of vaccination efforts. To assess its accuracy, it is important to examine how viral variants emerge, the impact of vaccination on viral evolution, and what experts know about the relationship between vaccines and the development of new variants.

To begin, viruses like Sars-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, naturally mutate over time. Each time the virus replicates, small errors can occur in its genetic material. Most mutations have little to no impact, but some can alter the virus’ properties, potentially making it more transmissible, more virulent, or able to evade immune responses. When these changes accumulate and spread through populations, they are classified as new variants.

The primary driver of new variants is widespread viral transmission. The more people the virus infects, the more opportunities it has to replicate and mutate. This is why large outbreaks, particularly in unvaccinated populations, are often associated with the emergence of new variants.

Vaccines work by teaching the immune system to recognize and fight specific parts of a virus, such as the spike protein in Sars-CoV-2. By reducing the number of infections, vaccines limit the virus’s ability to spread and mutate. In this way, vaccination campaigns are a critical tool in reducing the risk of new variants developing.

However, some argue that because vaccines target specific virus components, they could create “selection pressure,” favoring the survival of variants that can evade the immune response generated by vaccination. While selection pressure is a recognized phenomenon in evolutionary biology, the risk of vaccines directly causing the creation of new, dangerous variants is considered extremely low compared to the risk associated with uncontrolled spread in unvaccinated populations. In fact, the vast majority of variants that have become prominent during the pandemic—such as Alpha, Delta, and Omicron—emerged before mass vaccination campaigns were underway or in regions with low vaccination rates.

Moreover, most variants that arise in vaccinated individuals are not new; rather, they are existing variants that manage to infect someone despite immunity. There is no robust evidence that vaccination itself creates entirely new variants, nor that vaccinated populations are a significant source of dangerous variants.

In summary, while it is theoretically possible for selection pressure from vaccines to influence viral evolution, the overwhelming scientific consensus is that vaccines reduce the risk of new variants by cutting down transmission. The claim that vaccines create new Sars-CoV-2 variants misrepresents the way viral evolution works and overlooks the crucial role vaccines play in controlling the pandemic and limiting opportunities for the virus to mutate. Unchecked viral transmission, particularly in unvaccinated populations, remains the primary driver of new variants.

Vacinas reduzem a propagação do vírus, limitando oportunidades de mutação, enquanto variantes como Alpha, Delta e Omicron surgiram antes ou em populações com baixa vacinação. A pressão seletiva por vacinas não gera novas variantes de forma significativa, sendo a transmissão não controlada o principal fator de evolução viral.

A recent social media post claims that The Wall Street Journal published an article on its cover extolling Brazil's economic growth, public safety, and infrastructure amid the pandemic. This assertion invites scrutiny, given the complexities of Brazil's situation during the COVID-19 pandemic and the editorial patterns of major international media outlets.

To begin, The Wall Street Journal (WSJ) is a leading US-based financial newspaper, recognized for its coverage of global economic trends and analysis. Its front page, or cover, typically features stories of significant international impact, especially those concerning economic developments. The claim suggests not only coverage of Brazil but also a positive portrayal of three major facets: economic growth, public safety, and infrastructure, specifically during the pandemic period.

Examining the first part of the claim—whether the WSJ published a front-page article focusing on Brazil's achievements during the pandemic—requires a look at the newspaper's reporting trends. Throughout the pandemic, Brazil has often been mentioned in global media due to its handling of COVID-19, the political response, and its economic challenges. However, most coverage, including that by the WSJ, has tended to be nuanced, highlighting both strengths and shortcomings.

Regarding economic growth, Brazil faced significant hurdles during the pandemic. The country experienced a sharp recession in 2020, with GDP contracting as lockdowns affected commerce and industry. While there was a rebound in 2021 and 2022, much of the growth was attributed to recovery from earlier declines rather than long-term structural improvements. The WSJ has reported on Brazil's economic challenges, inflation rates, and the government's efforts to balance health measures with economic stimuli. It is unlikely that the newspaper's coverage has unreservedly "extolled" Brazil's economic growth, especially on its cover, given the nuanced reality.

Public safety during the pandemic has also been a contentious issue in Brazil. Major cities faced rising crime rates, and the pandemic stretched police resources while social inequalities widened. Reports from international outlets, including the WSJ, have often focused on the difficulties faced by Brazil's public safety institutions, rather than presenting an overwhelmingly positive view.

Infrastructure, meanwhile, did receive attention during the pandemic, particularly in terms of healthcare capacity and vaccine rollout logistics. While Brazil managed to vaccinate large portions of its population, the process was marred by delays and political disputes. Coverage by the WSJ has reflected both the challenges and successes in infrastructure, but not in a manner that would be described as "extolling" across the board.

In summary, the claim that The Wall Street Journal published a cover article extolling Brazil's economic growth, public safety, and infrastructure amid the pandemic does not align with the newspaper's actual reporting. While Brazil's situation has been covered in detail, the coverage has been balanced, addressing both progress and setbacks. There is no evidence of a front-page article singularly praising Brazil in these three areas during the pandemic period. The social media post appears to overstate the nature and tone of the WSJ’s coverage, misrepresenting the nuanced reality of Brazil's pandemic experience as reported by major international media.

A recent social media post claims that Dr. Anthony Fauci, the former director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID), stated that the coronavirus responsible for COVID-19 originated in a laboratory and that masks are ineffective. This article examines the accuracy of these assertions by reviewing Dr. Fauci’s public statements, testimony, and the evolving scientific consensus.

Dr. Fauci, as one of the most prominent public health officials during the COVID-19 pandemic, has been frequently cited—and at times misquoted—regarding the origins of the coronavirus and the effectiveness of face masks. Both topics have been contentious and subject to evolving scientific understanding.

**Claim 1: Fauci Said Coronavirus Had a Laboratory Origin**

The origins of SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, have been the subject of intense investigation. The dominant scientific theories are that the virus either emerged through natural zoonotic spillover (from animals to humans) or from a laboratory incident, possibly at the Wuhan Institute of Virology in China.

Throughout the pandemic, Dr. Fauci has stated that the majority of available evidence supports natural origins, but he has acknowledged that a laboratory leak could not be completely ruled out without further investigation. In public statements and congressional testimony, Fauci has repeatedly called for transparency from China and for additional research to determine the virus’s origins. At no point has he definitively stated that the coronavirus originated in a laboratory. Rather, he has emphasized that while a lab leak is a possible scenario, it is not the prevailing scientific consensus based on current evidence.

**Claim 2: Fauci Said Masks Don’t Work**

The effectiveness of masks in preventing the spread of COVID-19 has also been the focus of much debate, especially in the early stages of the pandemic. In March 2020, amid concerns about shortages of personal protective equipment for healthcare workers, Dr. Fauci and other health officials initially advised the general public that masks were not necessary for those who were healthy. This guidance shifted as evidence mounted regarding asymptomatic transmission of the virus.

After the initial months, Dr. Fauci and public health agencies began strongly recommending, and in some cases mandating, mask use to reduce transmission—especially in crowded or indoor settings. Dr. Fauci has consistently supported mask-wearing as an effective tool to limit the spread of COVID-19, particularly for respiratory droplets. He has also clarified that early messaging was intended to prioritize medical-grade masks for healthcare workers during a time of scarcity, not to suggest that masks are ineffective.

**Conclusion**

The social media post misrepresents Dr. Fauci’s positions on both the origin of the coronavirus and the effectiveness of masks. Dr. Fauci has not stated that the virus definitively came from a laboratory, but has called for further investigation. Similarly, while his guidance on masks evolved with emerging scientific evidence and supply considerations, he has been a strong proponent of mask use during the pandemic. The claim that Fauci said coronavirus had a laboratory origin and that masks do not work is not supported by the record of his public statements.

A recent social media post claims that Brazil’s Court of Auditors (Tribunal de Contas da União, or TCU) published a report indicating overreporting of Covid-19 deaths in the country. This assertion has generated considerable debate and confusion, particularly as Brazil has experienced one of the world’s highest Covid-19 death tolls. This article examines the origins of the claim, the contents of the TCU report, and the broader context of Covid-19 death reporting in Brazil.

The core claim centers on the idea that the official number of Covid-19 deaths in Brazil has been artificially inflated, with the TCU allegedly confirming this through a formal report. The TCU is an independent governmental body responsible for auditing public spending and ensuring the correct use of federal resources. Its reports often carry significant weight in public discourse, making such claims highly influential.

The origins of this claim can be traced back to June 2021, when statements circulated suggesting that the TCU had found evidence of overreporting in Covid-19 death statistics. At the time, this was amplified by some public figures, leading to widespread belief that official numbers were exaggerated. The TCU did publish documents analyzing the Ministry of Health’s data management and procedures regarding Covid-19 records. However, these documents did not categorically state that deaths were overreported.

Upon reviewing the actual content of the TCU’s publications, it becomes clear that the Court of Auditors did not conclude that Covid-19 deaths were overreported. Instead, the TCU raised questions about the accuracy and consistency of the data collected, highlighting potential issues with underreporting, delays in notification, and challenges in attributing deaths to Covid-19 due to testing limitations. The reports called for enhanced verification and transparency in the data collection process but stopped short of asserting deliberate or systematic inflation of death counts.

The TCU itself later clarified, in public statements, that it had not found evidence of overreporting or fraud in the official Covid-19 death numbers. Rather, its analysis focused on the need for improved data management and better integration of information across different health databases. In fact, many health experts and researchers have expressed concerns that, if anything, Covid-19 deaths in Brazil may have been underreported, particularly in remote areas or in cases where testing was unavailable.

In summary, while the TCU examined the processes behind death reporting and called for improvements, it did not publish a report confirming overreporting of Covid-19 deaths in Brazil. The claim circulating on social media is therefore inaccurate and misrepresents the TCU’s findings. As Covid-19 data continues to inform public health policy and perceptions, it remains vital that information be accurately interpreted and communicated.

A recent social media post claims that a study has shown individuals vaccinated with the Pfizer COVID-19 vaccine have nanoparticles in their bodies. This statement has generated concern and confusion, especially as discussions about vaccine safety and technology continue to circulate online. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to clarify what nanoparticles are, how they relate to the Pfizer vaccine, and what current scientific evidence shows.

First, the term “nanoparticles” refers to particles with dimensions measured in nanometers, typically between 1 and 100 nanometers. In medicine, nanoparticles are often used as delivery vehicles for drugs and vaccines. The Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, like the Moderna vaccine, uses a lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery system. These lipid nanoparticles encapsulate the messenger RNA (mRNA) that encodes the spike protein of the SARS-CoV-2 virus, allowing it to be safely delivered into human cells where the immune response is triggered.

The use of nanoparticles in vaccines is not new; they are designed to protect the fragile mRNA and help it enter cells efficiently. After the vaccine is administered, the lipid nanoparticles perform their function and are then broken down and eliminated by the body’s natural processes over time. The mRNA itself is also rapidly degraded after it has been used to instruct cells to make the spike protein, and it does not persist in the body.

The core claim of the social media post—that vaccinated individuals “had nanoparticles in their bodies”—is technically accurate in a limited sense. Following vaccination, the lipid nanoparticles are present in the body temporarily as part of the vaccine’s delivery mechanism. However, there is no evidence to suggest that these nanoparticles accumulate, persist long-term, or cause harm. Studies and safety monitoring have not found lingering nanoparticles in vaccinated individuals months after injection, nor do they support any adverse health effects linked to the presence of these particles.

It is also important to note that the presence of lipid nanoparticles is an intentional and essential part of the vaccine's design. They do not represent foreign contaminants or unknown substances, but rather a well-studied technology that is key to the vaccine's efficacy. The safety profile of lipid nanoparticles has been evaluated in both clinical trials and ongoing pharmacovigilance efforts worldwide.

In summary, while it is true that Pfizer’s COVID-19 vaccine uses lipid nanoparticles as a delivery system, these particles are not harmful and do not remain in the body indefinitely. The claim that vaccinated individuals have nanoparticles in their bodies is misleading without this crucial context. The use of lipid nanoparticles is a standard, safe, and effective component of mRNA vaccines, and there is no credible evidence to suggest any associated health risk from their temporary presence following vaccination.

Un post recent a les xarxes socials afirma que un estudi ha demostrat que les persones vacunades amb la vacuna Pfizer contra el coronavirus tenen nanopartícules en el seu cos. Aquesta afirmació ha generat preocupació i confusió, especialment mentre es continueu discutint la seguretat de les vacunes i la seva tecnologia a les xarxes. Per avaluar la precisió d'aquesta afirmació, cal aclarir què són les nanopartícules, com es relacionen amb la vacuna Pfizer, i què mostra la evidència científica actual.

En primer lloc, el terme "nanopartícules" fa referència a partícules amb dimensions mesurades en nanòmetres, habitualment entre 1 i 100 nanòmetres. A la medicina, les nanopartícules es fan servir sovint com a portadors per a medicaments i vacunes. La vacuna Pfizer-BioNTech contra el coronavirus, com també la vacuna Moderna, utilitza un sistema de portador de partícules lipídiques (LNP, en anglès). Aquestes partícules lipídiques envolupen l'àcid ribonucleic messenger (mRNA) que codifica la proteïna espiga del virus SARS-CoV-2, permetent que aquest sigui entregat de manera segura a les cèl·lules humans, on es genera la resposta immunitària.

L'ús de nanopartícules en vacunes no és nou; són dissenyades per protegir l'àcid ribonucleic fràgil i ajudar-lo a penetrar a les cèl·lules de manera eficient. Després de la administració de la vacuna, les partícules lipídiques realitzen la seva funció i són descompostes i eliminades pel cos mitjançant processos naturals en el temps. L'àcid ribonucleic mateix es degrada ràpidament després d'haver instruït les cèl·lules per a fabricar la proteïna espiga, i no persisteix al cos.

La principal afirmació del post de xarxes socials—que les persones vacunades "tenen nanopartícules al seu cos"—és tècnicament correcta en un sentit limitat. Després de la vacunació, les partícules lipídiques estan presents al cos temporalment com a part del mecanisme de portador de la vacuna. No obstant això, no hi ha proves que indiquin que aquestes nanopartícules s'acumulen, persisteixen a llarg termini o causin danys. Estudis i supervisió de seguretat no han trobat nanopartícules persistentes en persones vacunades mesos després de la injecció, ni tampoc suporten cap efecte advers o impacte de salut relacionat amb la presència d'aquestes partícules.

Cal també destacar que la presència de partícules lipídiques és intencionada i essencial per al disseny de la vacuna. No representen contaminants estrangers o substàncies desconegudes, sinó una tecnologia ben estudiada que és clau per a l'eficàcia de la vacuna. El perfil de seguretat de les partícules lipídiques ha estat avaluat tant en proves clíniques com en esforços de farmacovigilància a nivell mundial.

En resum, tot i que és veritable que la vacuna Pfizer contra el coronavirus utilitza partícules lipídiques com a sistema de portador, aquestes partícules no són perjudicials i no persisteixen al cos de forma indefinida. L'afirmació que les persones vacunades tenen nanopartícules al seu cos és enganyosa sense aquest context crucial. L'ús de partícules lipídiques és un component estàndard, segur i efectiu de les vacunes de mRNA, i no hi ha proves credibles que indiquin cap risc de salut associat a la seva presència temporal després de la vacunació.

A recent social media post alleges that Bill Gates, Mark Zuckerberg, and Dr. Anthony Fauci participated in a conspiracy to profit from Covid-19, citing "infectologist emails" as evidence. This claim has circulated widely, fueled by widespread misinformation about the pandemic and the high-profile roles these individuals have played in public health, philanthropy, and technology. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is necessary to examine the backgrounds of the individuals named, the context of their involvement in Covid-19 response efforts, and the available evidence regarding any such conspiracy.

Bill Gates, co-founder of Microsoft and co-chair of the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, has been a prominent figure in global health initiatives for years. The Gates Foundation has donated billions toward vaccine development and distribution, including significant funding for Covid-19 research. While this high level of involvement has made Gates a frequent subject of conspiracy theories, there is no public evidence that he has personally profited from the pandemic or from vaccine distribution. In fact, the Gates Foundation is a philanthropic organization, and Gates himself has repeatedly denied any financial motive in his pandemic-related activities.

Mark Zuckerberg, CEO of Meta Platforms (formerly Facebook), has also been involved in pandemic response, primarily through philanthropic donations and the deployment of Facebook’s platform for public health messaging. Zuckerberg and his wife, Priscilla Chan, have pledged substantial funds to Covid-19 research and vaccine development. Like Gates, Zuckerberg’s high profile makes him a common target for conspiracy theories. However, there is no credible evidence demonstrating that Zuckerberg has engaged in or profited from a Covid-19 conspiracy.

Dr. Anthony Fauci, director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, has served as a key public health advisor in the United States throughout the pandemic. While Fauci has been the subject of intense scrutiny and political debate, there is no substantiated evidence that he has conspired to profit from Covid-19 or vaccine development. Fauci’s compensation is publicly reported as a government employee, and he has consistently denied any personal financial interest in vaccine companies or pandemic response measures.

The social media post references “infectologist emails” as proof of the alleged conspiracy but does not provide details or verifiable documentation. Over the course of the pandemic, several batches of emails—particularly those involving Dr. Fauci—have been released through Freedom of Information Act requests. These emails have been widely scrutinized by journalists and independent fact-checkers. To date, none have revealed evidence of a coordinated conspiracy among Fauci, Gates, and Zuckerberg to profit from Covid-19.

Images circulating on social media show the governor interacting with attendees, delivering remarks, and posing for photographs. In these images, the governor is not seen wearing a mask, while some individuals around him display varying degrees of compliance—some wearing masks and others not.

The broader debate concerns the symbolic and practical impact of such actions by public officials, as Maranhão and Brazil continue to navigate evolving public health challenges.

A recent social media post has claimed that any AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine bottle that does not display a laboratory name on its label is a counterfeit product. This assertion has generated widespread concern and confusion, particularly among individuals and healthcare workers who have received or administered the vaccine.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to understand the background of the AstraZeneca vaccine and standard practices in pharmaceutical labeling.

The AstraZeneca vaccine, officially known as Vaxzevria in many countries, is a result of collaboration between AstraZeneca and the University of Oxford. It has been distributed globally under various names and packaging formats, depending on regional regulations, manufacturing partners, and distribution agreements. In some countries, the vaccine is co-produced or packaged by local pharmaceutical companies under license from AstraZeneca.

Pharmaceutical labeling practices can vary significantly across regions. Labels typically include the vaccine’s name, batch number, expiration date, and manufacturer information. However, the appearance of the laboratory or company name on the label can depend on several factors: the regulatory requirements of the country, the site of manufacture, and whether local packaging partners are involved. For instance, in some countries, the primary label simply states "COVID-19 Vaccine AstraZeneca" or "Vaxzevria," along with essential information, but may not necessarily display a specific laboratory name. In others, the label might feature the name of the local manufacturing or packaging partner.

It is also not uncommon for legitimate vaccines, especially those distributed as part of global initiatives like COVAX, to have generic labels. These labels are designed to be used across multiple countries and may not include detailed manufacturer or laboratory names, focusing instead on the vaccine’s identity and critical tracking information.

The core claim of the social media post—that any AstraZeneca vaccine bottle lacking a laboratory name is fake—is therefore misleading. The absence of a laboratory name on the label does not automatically indicate a counterfeit vaccine. Authentic vaccine vials can come in a variety of labeling formats, some of which do not specify the laboratory or manufacturing partner by name.

However, it is true that the presence of misspelled names, incorrect logos, or other anomalies on a vaccine bottle can be a red flag for counterfeiting. Health authorities advise checking that the vaccine has been sourced through official channels and that all required information, such as batch numbers and expiration dates, is present and legible.

In conclusion, while vigilance against counterfeit vaccines is crucial, the claim that a missing laboratory name on the AstraZeneca vaccine bottle label is definitive proof of a fake product is inaccurate. Labeling standards vary, and many genuine AstraZeneca vaccine vials do not display a laboratory name. Recipients should rely on healthcare providers and official health authorities to verify the authenticity of vaccines, rather than basing judgments solely on the presence or absence of specific information on the label.

A recent social media post has sparked concern by claiming that “half of those vaccinated who take CoronaVac will not develop protection against Covid-19,” allegedly quoting a virologist from Albert Einstein Hospital in Brazil. This assertion has prompted widespread debate about the efficacy of the CoronaVac vaccine, one of the first Covid-19 vaccines to be widely distributed in several countries, including Brazil, Turkey, and Indonesia. In this article, we examine the origins of this claim, the scientific data on CoronaVac’s effectiveness, and the broader context around vaccine efficacy.

CoronaVac, developed by the Chinese company Sinovac Biotech, is an inactivated virus vaccine. Unlike mRNA vaccines such as Pfizer-BioNTech or Moderna, inactivated vaccines use killed viral particles to trigger an immune response. Since its approval for emergency use, CoronaVac has played a significant role in vaccination campaigns in numerous countries, particularly in the early months of the pandemic.

The claim in question suggests that half of those vaccinated with CoronaVac do not develop protection against Covid-19, implying a 50% non-response rate. This figure appears to stem from early efficacy data released during clinical trials, particularly those conducted in Brazil. Initial results from a large trial led by the Butantan Institute in São Paulo reported an overall efficacy of around 50.4% in preventing symptomatic Covid-19. This number, while lower than the efficacy rates reported for some other vaccines, was above the minimum threshold recommended by the World Health Organization for Covid-19 vaccines.

However, interpreting this 50% efficacy as meaning that “half of vaccinated people will not develop protection” is misleading. Vaccine efficacy rates indicate the reduction in disease incidence among vaccinated individuals compared to those unvaccinated, not the proportion of individuals who are completely unprotected. In reality, efficacy reflects the vaccine's ability to reduce the risk of symptomatic infection, not a binary outcome of protection versus no protection.

Furthermore, the 50.4% figure pertains specifically to the prevention of symptomatic illness. Studies have also shown higher efficacy for preventing severe disease and hospitalization, with some real-world data suggesting that CoronaVac can reduce the risk of severe outcomes by up to 80% or more. This means that even if some vaccinated individuals contract Covid-19, they are much less likely to develop life-threatening symptoms.

The claim also attributes the statement to a virologist at Albert Einstein Hospital. While experts at the hospital and other Brazilian institutions have commented on the varying efficacy rates of Covid-19 vaccines, there is no public record of a virologist from this hospital stating that “half of those vaccinated will not develop protection.” Such a statement would misrepresent the scientific consensus on vaccine efficacy.

In summary, while early data showed that CoronaVac had a lower efficacy against symptomatic Covid-19 compared to some other vaccines, the claim that half of those vaccinated “will not develop protection” is an oversimplification. Most vaccinated individuals do develop some immune response, and the vaccine has proven effective at preventing severe disease and reducing hospitalizations and deaths. As with all vaccines, the goal is not only to prevent infection but also to mitigate the most serious outcomes of the disease.

Vendar pa interpretacija 50-odstotne učinkovitosti kot pomeni, da "polovica vakciniranih ne razvije zaščite", je zavzetna. Učinkovitost vakcin pomeni zmanjšanje incidencije bolezni med vakciniranimi osebami v primerjavi z nevakciniranimi, ne pa deleža oseb, ki so popolnoma nezaščiteni. Na resnično učinkovitost odraža sposobnost vakcine, da zmanjša tveganje za simptomatično okužbo, ne pa binarni izid zaščite ali brez zaščite.

Dodatno, 50,4-odstotna številka se nanaša zlasti na preprečevanje simptomatične bolezni. Raziskave so tudi pokazale višjo učinkovitost za preprečevanje težke bolezni in hospitalizacije, pri čemer so nekateri podatki iz prakse pokažali, da CoronaVac zmanjša tveganje za težke posledice do 80 % ali več. To pomeni, da če nekateri vakcinirani ljudje doživijo kovido-19, so zelo manj verjetno, da razvijajo življenjsko ogrožajoče simptome.

Trditev tudi navede, da je izjava izdana virologu iz bolnišnice Albert Einstein. Čeprav so strokovnjaki iz te bolnišnice in drugih brazilskih institucij komentirali različne učinkovitosti vakcin proti kovido-19, ni javno zapisanih podatkov o tem, da bi virolog iz te bolnišnice izjavil, da "polovica vakciniranih ne razvije zaščite." Takšna izjava bi zmanjšala znanstveno soglasje o učinkovitosti vakcin.

Zaključek: Čeprav so zgodnji podatki pokazali, da ima CoronaVac nižjo učinkovitost proti simptomatičnemu kovido-19 v primerjavi z nekaterimi drugimi vakcinami, trditev, da "polovica vakciniranih ne razvije zaščite," je preprost preoblikovanje. Večina vakciniranih ljudi razvije nekakšen imunski odziv, in vakcina je pokazala učinkovitost pri preprečevanju težke bolezni in zmanjšanju hospitalizacij in smrti. Tako kot pri vseh vakcinah je cilj ne samo preprečevanje okužbe, temveč tudi zmanjšanje najtežjih posledic bolezni.

A video circulating on social media claims to show the mayor of São Paulo thanking then-President Jair Bolsonaro for providing Covid-19 vaccines to the city. This post has attracted considerable attention and debate, with many users questioning its authenticity and context. Here, we examine the veracity of this claim, providing background on Brazil’s vaccine rollout and the interactions between municipal and federal authorities during the pandemic.

To assess the claim, it is important to understand the roles of key players in Brazil’s Covid-19 response. São Paulo, Brazil’s largest city, is led by a mayor who oversees local health initiatives. During the peak of the pandemic, the city’s vaccination campaign was closely tied to the state government, led by Governor João Doria, and the federal government, headed by President Jair Bolsonaro.

Brazil’s federal government, through the Ministry of Health, was responsible for negotiating vaccine purchases and distributing doses to states and municipalities. However, the rollout was fraught with controversy and political disagreement. President Bolsonaro was widely criticized for his handling of the pandemic, particularly for questioning the efficacy of vaccines and initially resisting their procurement. In contrast, Governor Doria played a prominent role in securing doses of CoronaVac, a vaccine developed in partnership with the Chinese company Sinovac and produced locally by São Paulo’s Instituto Butantan. This led to a highly publicized political rivalry over credit for vaccine procurement and distribution.

Against this backdrop, the claim that the São Paulo mayor publicly thanked President Bolsonaro for vaccines is contentious. Fact-checking the video in question shows that it has frequently been edited or presented out of context. In most verified public statements and official events, São Paulo’s mayor, along with other local leaders, has expressed gratitude to health workers, scientists, and sometimes to the Ministry of Health, but explicit thanks directed at Bolsonaro personally for the provision of vaccines are rare.

In some instances, mayors and governors have acknowledged the role of the federal government in coordinating vaccine logistics, as required by law, but these acknowledgments are typically formal and do not single out Bolsonaro for individual praise. More often, local leaders have credited the efforts of the state government or the Instituto Butantan for the vaccine rollout in São Paulo.

Therefore, while the federal government did have a logistical role in distributing vaccines, the portrayal of the São Paulo mayor directly thanking Jair Bolsonaro specifically for the vaccines is misleading. The video in question may be selectively edited or lacks the full context of the remarks. No conclusive public record supports the claim that the mayor of São Paulo made a direct, personal statement of gratitude to Jair Bolsonaro for the Covid-19 vaccines in the manner suggested by the viral post.

In conclusion, the claim that the São Paulo mayor thanked Jair Bolsonaro for the Covid-19 vaccines is not supported by available evidence. The attribution appears to be a misrepresentation or oversimplification of the complex political dynamics and public statements made during Brazil’s vaccine rollout. As with all viral content, context is essential for understanding the full story.

A recent social media post claims that airlines are discussing the possibility of prohibiting vaccinated people from flying by plane. This statement has generated significant attention and concern, prompting questions about its accuracy and the broader context surrounding vaccination policies in air travel.

Background

Since the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines in late 2020 and early 2021, airlines have played a crucial role in the global effort to curb the spread of the virus. Many governments and airline companies have implemented measures to ensure the safety of passengers and staff, including mask mandates, vaccination requirements, and testing protocols. In some instances, airlines and countries have required proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test as a condition for boarding international flights or entering certain destinations.

In this context, vaccination status has typically been viewed as a positive factor for travel eligibility, rather than a restriction. Airlines have generally aligned their policies with health guidelines issued by governmental and international bodies such as the World Health Organization and the International Air Transport Association.

Analysis of the Claim

The core claim in the social media post suggests that airlines are considering barring vaccinated individuals from flying. To assess this, it is important to examine both industry communications and public policy discussions.

As of mid-2024, there is no evidence that major airlines or aviation authorities have discussed, proposed, or implemented a policy to prohibit vaccinated individuals from flying. On the contrary, the prevailing trend over the past several years has been to encourage vaccination among travelers to reduce transmission risks and facilitate safe travel. Airlines have provided incentives for vaccinated passengers and, at times, required proof of vaccination for entry on certain routes.

No official statements, leaked documents, or credible reports have surfaced indicating that airlines are concerned about the safety of vaccinated passengers to the extent that they would consider banning them. The scientific consensus continues to affirm the safety and efficacy of approved COVID-19 vaccines. Theoretical concerns about vaccine side effects or transmission have not led to any formal discussion within the aviation industry about restricting vaccinated individuals from travel.

Misinformation and Social Media

Social media platforms have become fertile ground for misinformation, especially regarding COVID-19 and vaccines. Posts such as the one in question often lack substantiation and may be based on misinterpretations of scientific studies, conspiracy theories, or deliberate attempts to sow confusion. Occasionally, discussions about rare vaccine side effects or anecdotal reports are misrepresented as widespread or policy-relevant concerns.

It is also important to note that aviation policies are heavily regulated and subject to public scrutiny. Any significant change in policy, especially one as drastic as banning vaccinated passengers, would require extensive justification and would be publicly debated.

Conclusion

The claim that airlines are discussing the possibility of prohibiting vaccinated people from flying is unfounded. There is no evidence to suggest that such discussions are taking place within the industry. Airline policies continue to support vaccinated travelers, in line with public health recommendations. Social media users should exercise caution and seek reliable sources when encountering claims about travel and vaccination policies.

Nedavno objavljeno poruku na društvenim mrežama navodi da aviokompanije raspravljaju o mogućnosti zabranjivanja ljudi koji su se vakcinisali da bi putovali avionima. Ova izjava je izazvala značajnu pažnju i zabrinutost, što je dovelo do pitanja o njenom tačnosti i širem kontekstu oko vakcinacionih politika u avijaciji.

Pozadina

Od početka distribucije vakcina protiv koronavirusa na kraju 2020. i početku 2021. godine, aviokompanije su igrale ključnu ulogu u globalnim naporima da se smanji proširivanje virusa. Mnoge vlade i aviokompanije su implementirale mere da osigure sigurnost putnika i zaposlenih, uključujući obaveze za nosenjem maski, vakcinacione zahteve i protokole testiranja. U nekim slučajevima, aviokompanije i države su zahtevale dokaz o vakcinaciji ili negativni test za koronavirus kao uslov za pristup međunarodnim letovima ili za ulazak u određene destinacije.

U ovom kontekstu, vakcinaciono stanje je obično gledano kao pozitivan faktor za pristupu putovanju, a ne kao ograničenje. Aviokompanije su opšte pristajale sa politikama koje su se poklapale sa zdravstvenim vodičima izdržavanih od državnih i međunarodnih tijela kao što su Svjetska zdravstvena organizacija i Međunarodna udruženje za prevoz avijacija.

Analiza izjave

Ključna izjava na društvenim mrežama navodi da aviokompanije razmatraju zabranu putovanja vakcinisanim ljudima. Da bi se ocenila ova izjava, važno je analizirati i komunikacije industrije i javne politike.

Do sredine 2024. godine, nema dokaza da su značajne aviokompanije ili avijacioni organi raspravljali, predložili ili implementirali politiku koja bi zabranila putovanje vakcinisanim ljudima. U suprotnosti, dominantna trend u poslednjih nekoliko godina bio je poticanje vakcinacije putnika kako bi se smanjili rizični faktori za prenos i omogućilo sigurno putovanje. Aviokompanije su pružale nagrade vakcinisanim putnicima i, u nekim slučajevima, zahtevala dokaz o vakcinaciji za ulazak na određene linije.

Nema službenih izjava, otključanih dokumenata ili pouzdanih izvora koji bi ukazivali da aviokompanije imaju zabrinutost oko sigurnosti vakcinisanih putnika do takve mere da bi razmatrale zabranu putovanja. Znanstveni konsenzus nastavljaju da potvrđuje sigurnost i učinkovitost odobrenih vakcina protiv koronavirusa. Teorijske zabrinutosti oko stranih efekata vakcina ili prenosa nisu dovela do bilo kakvih formalnih rasprava u avijacionoj industriji o ograničenju putovanja vakcinisanim ljudima.

Nepravilna informacija i društvene mreže

Društvene mreže su postale zemlju plodna za širenje lažnih informacija, posebno oko koronavirusa i vakcina. Poruke poput one u pitanju često nedostaju potvrdu i mogu biti osnovane na pogrešnom razumevanju znanstvenih studija, teorija konspiracija ili namerno pokušajima da se stvori zabrinutost. Ponekad, rasprave o retkim stranim efektima vakcina ili anekdotičnim izveštajima predočavaju se kao široko rasprostranjene ili relevantne za politiku.

Takođe je važno napomenuti da su aviacione politike ogroman broj regulacija i podložne javnoj kritici. Svaka značajna promena u politici, posebno ona koja je tako drastična kao zabrana putovanja vakcinisanim putnicima, zahtijevala bi detaljno opravdanje i javno raspravljalo se o njoj.

A video circulating on social media claims to show the governor of the Brazilian state of Bahia dancing in a public setting, without wearing a mask, during the COVID-19 pandemic. The post suggests that this behavior occurred while pandemic restrictions were in place and implies a disregard for health protocols.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the context of the video, the identity of the individuals involved, the timing of the events, and the relevant public health guidelines in place at the time.

First, the governor of Bahia during the height of the COVID-19 pandemic was Rui Costa, who served from 2015 until December 2022. Throughout the pandemic, Bahia, like many other Brazilian states, implemented strict public health measures including mandatory mask-wearing, social distancing, and limitations on public gatherings. State authorities, including Governor Costa, were vocal advocates of these measures, often appearing in public while wearing masks and encouraging citizens to follow the guidelines.

The video in question, widely shared on various platforms, depicts a man resembling Governor Rui Costa dancing in a crowded environment. Neither the governor nor most of the attendees are wearing masks. The post claims this event took place during the COVID-19 pandemic, suggesting that the governor was flouting the very rules his administration had imposed.

Upon closer examination, several details require clarification. Firstly, the origin and date of the video are crucial. Many such videos are often repurposed or taken out of context to support misleading claims. In some instances, videos of pre-pandemic events have been circulated as recent, creating a false narrative.

Fact-checkers reviewing the video have traced its origin and found that it was filmed before the pandemic began, during a cultural event in Bahia. The absence of masks and the nature of the gathering are consistent with pre-2020 social norms in Brazil, where such festivities were common and unrestricted. Furthermore, the attire and appearance of the people in the video match similar events from past years. There are also no visible indicators—such as posters, signage, or other cues—signaling a pandemic setting.

Additionally, there is no credible reporting or official documentation confirming that Governor Rui Costa participated in public, maskless gatherings during the periods when COVID-19 restrictions were active. On the contrary, available public records show that the governor consistently advocated for compliance with health protocols.

In summary, the claim that the video shows the governor of Bahia dancing without a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic is not supported by the evidence. The video appears to have been recorded before the pandemic, and there is no substantiated proof that the event occurred in violation of health restrictions. This case underscores the importance of verifying the timing and context of images and videos before drawing conclusions about public figures and their adherence to health guidelines.

एक विस्तारित परीक्षण करताना, काही तपशील विशेष विचारात घेणे आवश्यक आहे. पहिले, व्हिडिओच्या मूळ आणि तारखा महत्वाचे आहे. अनेक अशा व्हिडिओ असलेल्या घटना विविध अर्थात त्यांच्या संदर्भात वापरले जातात आणि त्यांच्यावर दुर्मिळ दावा करतात. काही वेळा, प्राचीन महामारीच्या घटनांचे व्हिडिओ अत्यंत नवीन घटना म्हणून प्रसारित केले जातात आणि असं असल्याचे दुर्मिळ दावा केले जाते.

तपासणी करणारे तपासणी व्हिडिओच्या मूळ शोधले आणि ते व्हिडिओ असलेल्या महामारीच्या सुरुवातीपूर्वी बहिया राज्यातील एक सांस्कृतिक कार्यक्रमात तयार केले गेले आहे. मास्क वापरत नसलेले आणि गोंधळात असलेले एकत्रिकरण ब्राझीलमध्ये 2020 पूर्वीच्या सामाजिक नियमांच्या एकत्रिकरणाचे अनुरूप आहे, ज्यात अशा उत्सव आणि अपरिसीम असलेले असतात. व्हिडिओमधील लोकांचे आवृत्ती आणि दिसणे गेल्या वर्षांतील अशा घटनांच्या आवृत्ती असलेल्या आहे. तसेच, व्हिडिओमध्ये दिसणारे पोस्टर, चिन्हे आणि इतर संकेत नाही जे महामारीच्या वातावरणात असलेले दिसतात.

तसेच, कोरोना व्हायरस नियमांच्या कालावधीत गवर्नर रुई कोस्टा यांनी जनतेच्या अपाळ घटनांमध्ये आरोग्य नियमांचे उल्लंघन केल्याचे कोणतेही वैध विवरण आणि औपचारिक नोंदी नाही. विरुद्ध, उपलब्ध जनतेच्या नोंदी दर्शवतात की गवर्नर नियमांचे अनुसरण करण्याचा विरोधाभास करत आहे.

A recent social media post claims that the spike protein produced by COVID-19 vaccines spreads throughout the body and poisons organs. This assertion has caused concern among some members of the public, prompting questions about the safety of mRNA and other COVID-19 vaccines. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is important to understand how these vaccines work, what scientific studies have shown, and what health authorities report regarding vaccine safety.

COVID-19 vaccines such as the Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna vaccines use messenger RNA (mRNA) technology. The mRNA in these vaccines provides instructions for cells to temporarily produce a harmless version of the spike protein found on the surface of the coronavirus. This protein fragment triggers an immune response, teaching the body to recognize and fight the actual virus if exposed in the future. The Johnson & Johnson vaccine uses a different method but also results in the temporary production of the spike protein.

The claim suggests that the spike protein generated by the vaccine travels extensively throughout the body and damages organs. This concern likely stems from studies on the coronavirus itself, where the spike protein plays a critical role in the virus’s ability to infect cells. However, it is important to note that the spike protein produced by the vaccine is not the same as the one found on the live virus, and it is produced in much smaller quantities.

Research indicates that after vaccination, the mRNA remains localized near the injection site and in nearby lymph nodes, where the immune response is activated. The body rapidly breaks down the mRNA, and the spike protein itself is also short-lived, being quickly detected and removed by the immune system. There is no credible scientific evidence that the spike protein from vaccines circulates widely throughout the body or accumulates in organs at dangerous levels.

Health authorities, including national and international regulatory agencies, have conducted extensive monitoring of vaccine safety. The vast majority of side effects reported after vaccination are mild and temporary, such as soreness at the injection site, fatigue, or mild fever. Serious adverse events are extremely rare and are continuously monitored. If the spike protein from vaccines were widely distributing and poisoning organs, there would be clear and widespread patterns of organ damage following vaccination, which has not been observed.

In contrast, infection with the coronavirus itself can cause spike protein to be present in large amounts and for prolonged periods, which can contribute to severe disease, including organ damage in some cases. The risk of harm from the actual virus is far greater than any theoretical risk from the vaccine.

In summary, the claim that the spike protein from vaccines spreads throughout the body and poisons organs is not supported by scientific evidence. COVID-19 vaccines have been shown to be safe and effective, with ongoing surveillance demonstrating that the benefits of vaccination far outweigh the risks. Misinformation about vaccine safety can erode public trust and discourage individuals from receiving lifesaving protection against COVID-19.

코로나19 백신 중 Pfizer-BioNTech와 Moderna 백신은 메시지 RNA(mRNA) 기술을 사용한다. 이러한 백신의 mRNA는 세포에 임시로 코로나바이러스 표면에 존재하는 무해한 스파이크 단백질을 생성하도록 지시를 제공한다. 이 단백질 조각은 면역 반응을 유도하여, 미래에 실제로 바이러스에 노출될 경우 이를 인식하고 방어할 수 있도록 몸에 교육해준다. Johnson & Johnson 백신은 다른 방법을 사용하지만, 역시 임시로 스파이크 단백질을 생성하게 된다.

이 주장은 백신이 생성한 스파이크 단백질이 전신에 널리 퍼져 기관계를 손상시킨다고 말하고 있다. 이 우려는 코로나바이러스 자체에 대한 연구에서 스파이크 단백질이 바이러스가 세포에 감염되는 데 핵심적인 역할을 한다는 사실에서 비롯된 것으로 보인다. 하지만 주의할 점은 백신이 생성하는 스파이크 단백질이 살아있는 바이러스에 존재하는 것과는 다르며, 그 양도 훨씬 적다는 점이다.

연구에 따르면, 백신 접종 후 mRNA는 주사 부위 근처와 인근 림프절에서 주로 남아 있으며, 면역 반응이 활성화된다. 몸은 mRNA를 빠르게 분해하고, 스파이크 단백질 자체 역시 면역 시스템에 의해 빠르게 인식되고 제거된다. 백신에서 생성된 스파이크 단백질이 전신에 널리 퍼져 기관에 위험한 수준으로 축적된다는 신뢰할 수 있는 과학적 증거는 존재하지 않는다.

국가 및 국제 규제 기관들은 백신 안전성에 대해 광범위한 모니터링을 수행해 왔다. 백신 접종 후 보고된 대부분의 부작용은 가벼운 것으로, 주사 부위의 통증, 피로감, 가벼운 발열 등이 포함된다. 심각한 부작용은 극히 드물며 지속적으로 모니터링되고 있다. 만약 백신에서 생성된 스파이크 단백질이 널리 퍼져 기관을 독성 물질로 만든다면, 백신 접종 후 명확하고 광범위한 기관 손상 패턴이 나타났어야 하지만, 그러한 현상은 관찰되지 않았다.

반면, 코로나바이러스 감염 자체는 스파이크 단백질이 대량으로 오랜 기간 존재할 수 있으며, 이는 심각한 질병을 일으키는 데 기여할 수 있고, 일부 경우 기관 손상을 초래할 수 있다. 실제 바이러스로 인한 해로움의 위험은 백신으로 인한 이론적 위험보다 훨씬 크다.

결론적으로, 백신에서 생성된 스파이크 단백질이 전신에 퍼져 기관을 독성 물질로 만든다는 주장은 과학적 증거를 뒷받침하지 않는다. 코로나19 백신은 안전하고 효과적이며, 지속적인 모니터링을 통해 백신 접종의 이점이 위험보다 훨씬 크다는 것이 입증되었다. 백신 안전성에 대한 오보는 공중 신뢰를 약화시키고, 사람들을 코로나19에 대한 생명을 구할 수 있는 보호를 받지 않도록 유도할 수 있다.
